Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We suggest that future observations with augmented sensitivity and coverage are necessary to thoroughly explore anisotropy at the highest energy levels. Additionally, we highlight the necessity for simultaneous studies across multiple observational platforms. We also present initial findings regarding the spatial distribution of extremely energetic cosmic rays in right ascension and declination bands, which may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of cosmic ray anisotropy. Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$. Moreover, our results feature an interesting 'duality' where the'metrics' on the manifolds describe the motion of particles and fields. This is particularly evident in $su(2)$, where the tree-level $E_{ab}$ corresponds to the graviton metric. Conversely, the leading term at $\theta$ represents the Yang-Mills field on the $S^3$ manifold. Thus, our model may serve as a bridge connecting general relativity and Yang-Mills theory in the framework of noncommutative geometry. Finally, our analysis suggests that the Dirac operator in a noncommutative torus can be represented as a linear differential operator in the momentum space, linking this problem to the study of the Berry phase in flat spaces. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further explore the benefits of federated learning in this domain, we conducted an additional study in which we trained a model to distinguish between different tumor grades using data from The Cancer Genome Atlas. Our results show that federated learning can yield models with high accuracy across various tumor grades, even in scenarios where data is highly imbalanced. These outcomes demonstrate the potential of federated learning to facilitate the development of high-performance image analysis models for cancer diagnosis, overcoming challenges associated with collecting large, diverse datasets. To facilitate replication and advancement of our studies, we are making the code and models developed as part of this research publicly available. This includes the code used for data simulation, model training, and evaluation, as well as the models themselves, which can be accessed via the provided link in the paper. Through our experiments, we also explored the influence of different hyperparameters on the performance of federated learning, finding that performance can vary significantly depending on the specific approach used, and highlighting the need for further research to fully optimize performance across different datasets and applications. Finally, we outline potential directions for future research, including the application of federated learning to additional tasks, such as tissue segmentation. This could involve expanding the use of learning algorithms beyond classification, and incorporating additional types of data, such as genomic data, to enhance the accuracy of cancer diagnosis. Ultimately, our findings suggest that federated learning has significant potential to facilitate the development of accurate, reliable, and high-performance image analysis models for cancer diagnosis, while protecting sensitive medical data. The proposed WDFFE-MLSE method also offered a key benefit of low computational complexity. The findings of this study are further validated by means of Monte Carlo simulations. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've demonstrated the efficacy of this approach on diverse time-series datasets on two prominent benchmark platforms. Our technique is versatile and can be integrated with various TCN architectures, activation functions, and loss functions. The advantages of this method include a substantial reduction in model size, increased accuracy in some cases, and the capability to generate a range of efficient TCN models suitable for a range of inference throughput requirements. Furthermore, the model sizes produced by this method have competitive performance in real-world embedded AI applications. We've also introduced a new state-of-the-art model that surpasses the previous design in both efficiency and accuracy and has been integrated into an open-source deep learning framework. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. Additionally, our work identifies the dimension of a specific irreducible representation of the generalized Jordanian twist algebra, and we establish the connection between the dimension of a Zinbiel algebra and that of its twist algebra. Our proof involves establishing the compatibility of the Zinbiel algebra operation with the generalized Jordanian twist algebra, enabling us to determine the dimension of a particular irreducible representation. Consequently, our results allow us to derive the dimension of the Zinbiel algebra itself. This leads to the conclusion that the dimension of the twist algebra is proportional to the square of the dimension of the Zinbiel algebra. Lastly, we establish the solvability of the twist algebra by demonstrating the nilpotency of the Zinbiel algebra. This research was initially presented at the 109th Section Meeting of the Japanese Mathematical Society, held from July 19-20, 2019, at Nagoya University.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Additionally, this new technique paves the way for future studies on the fundamental interactions between particles and the characteristics of the quark--gluon plasma in collisions of various energies and different types of ions. Lastly, it enables comparisons to theoretical models with a higher degree of precision, which is crucial for developing a comprehensive and precise understanding of these complex collisions. These new insights, along with fresh perspectives on the composition of quark--gluon plasma and the behavior of particles as a function of the temperature and chemical potential of the system, will continue to shape the field of heavy-ion physics. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse engineering of the ALBA algorithm for DLEs can be viewed as an instance of a known result from the theory of term rewriting systems, specifically the theorem that any application of a left-linear term rewriting system has a corresponding reverse derivation. Building upon this foundation, we establish a key insight into the algebraic structure of DLE and its connections to the ALBA rules to demonstrate the validity of our proposed method in the DLE setting. Furthermore, we extend this approach to logics whose semantics are based on order-theoretic structures more complex than normal lattice expansions, namely multi-sorted DLEs (MDE). This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. We also provide an efficient algorithm for our proposed strategy and showcase its effectiveness through practical applications. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. The results of our analysis have indicated a strong forecast accuracy of the TV-PARX model, surpassing both static models and alternatives focused on modeling time series persistence. The research is supported by the R package "tvparx", allowing users to estimate and forecast count-based time series data sets using the time-varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates model. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/. Our code is available at https://github.com/yilundu/ndf. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. To further investigate this observation, I plan to explore the co-authorship graph of the archive's contributors, examining the development of the graph over time and identifying clusters within it. To illustrate this approach, I plan to apply it to the Isabelle proof of the Prime Number Theorem, assessing the relevance of various components of the proof relative to its overall structure and identifying suggestions for improving the teaching of this concept. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. Furthermore, we have confirmed the critical exponent $\gamma$ to be in line with mean field theory's predictions for O(N) universality classes, also validating our approach by comparing it with the universal behavior described by the Derrida equation at $N=2$. Additionally, we have derived a universal relationship which may be useful in identifying the Yang-Lee edge singularity within a first-order phase transition's data by linking the critical exponent $\gamma$ to the critical exponent $\Delta$ of the leading infrared singularity in the thermodynamic limit via $\gamma = 1 / \Delta$. Lastly, we have assessed the Yang-Lee edge singularity's stability by estimating the magnitude of relevant operators in QCD's relevant universality classes, finding their effects to be highly suppressed as anticipated. A scale-free model serving as a proxy for our renormalization group study also enables us to illustrate the Yang-Lee edge singularity's origin through a momemtum-shell model. This study's results provide a significant improvement over earlier data and a more precise understanding of the Yang-Lee edge singularity within the O(N) universality classes for $N=2, 4$. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. These measurements enabled us to determine the optical depth with acceptable accuracy of 0.01 despite the systems' calibration differences. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code and models are available online at https://github.com/ChenZhSui/Direct-Pipeline-Refine.

Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting directions for enhanced understanding of fluid dynamics through peridynamics. This comprehensive review aims to provide a cohesive framework for bond-based peridynamic models, addressing both fundamental concepts and potential directions for further research. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. Moreover, it
includes an efficient matrix representation for Structural Equation Modeling,
introducing an innovative formulation for parameter estimation. The library
also provides an intuitive API and a comprehensive set of built-in tools for
model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and graphical results. Ultimately, the
GGLasso package aims to present a versatile framework that can be utilized as a
benchmark or a starting point for complex generalized graphical lasso challenges. The library is
available at https://github.com/RPVCians/GGLasso and can be installed via

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. Experimental results show that our model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both objective and subjective evaluations on real-world images. The proposed model's simplicity and efficacy make it suitable for a wide range of deblurring tasks. The code and data are available at https://github.com/zh117043119/RAW-SSDMR.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. This involves utilizing the deformed $R$-Minkowski spacetime and 
its associated non-standard deformed Dirac equation. We demonstrate that both equations 
are analogous and share the same normalized wave functions. This enables the direct 
utilization of solutions to the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime, which is 
a novel finding. We predict that this analogy will extend to other spin states and 
discuss potential directions for further investigation.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results demonstrated that a modest increase in training time allows the FPG algorithm to obtain robust policies comparable to those obtained in non-adversarial scenarios. The FPG algorithm is open to further development, representing a starting point for exploring other robust reinforcement learning methods. The code is available at https://github.com/hengryn/filtered_pgd. We also introduced a new metric, the robust success ratio (SR), to effectively evaluate the performance of agents in challenging tasks. We anticipate that this metric will be a valuable tool for comparing the robustness of agents in continuous control scenarios. We provided the FPG algorithm code, obtained novel benchmarks for the robust success ratio, and provided results for the miji-co benchmarks as part of this research. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Furthermore, we propose utilizing SPCCSs as a source for generating entangled states in optical networks. In this scenario, the catalytic device would generate both a catalyzed coherent state and a multi-photon entangled state, thereby facilitating the creation of entanglement without requiring initial access to single-photon states. This concept is exemplified by a diagram illustrating the generation of seed states for the circuit, and we anticipate that this approach will contribute to the development and scaling of optical quantum networks. These applications highlight the potential of single-photon catalyzed coherent states to play a significant role in optical quantum networks, especially when combined with other non-classical states generated through quantum-optical catalysis. Moreover, we explore the inherent robustness of SPCCSs to linear transformations and collection losses, showcasing their ability to maintain quantum properties even when subject to these types of noise. Ultimately, we propose employing SPCCSs as a quantum source for controlling the flow of photons in optical quantum circuits, thereby facilitating the efficient collection of entangled states. This approach is crucial for overcoming the constraints imposed by single-photon collection and enabling the scalable production of multi-photon entangled states in optical quantum networks. As such, we anticipate that single-photon catalyzed coherent states will play a pivotal role in optical quantum networks, contributing to the development of complex quantum operations required for these systems.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. Additionally, this method offers significant advantages in terms of speed, mounting it with multiple possible advantages over other methods such as the simultaneous use of multiple CPUs, allowing it to be an attractive option for complex well logging applications where high computational speed is mandatory. This paper confirms that the iterative least-squares method can result in tight ensembles, allowing for the construction of a highly accurate mean estimate, also confirming the capability of this method to handle complex well logging involving multiple layers, where other ensemble-based methods like Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo might struggle. We also introduce a new tool called the Standardized Boundary Error, a metric that evaluates the accuracy of layer boundary estimations, and validate this metric by comparing it with the widely used Bayesian probability, demonstrating that it offers a more transparent and straightforward way to assess the correctness of layer boundary estimations. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of using multiple receivers at each mobile node, as well as the effects of varying the density of the surrounding sensing nodes. Key to these investigations is a newly developed and highly efficient location detection algorithm, capable of running on a standard 8MB ZigBee coordinator device. We also present location estimation data obtained from outdoor field tests, conducted on a 150m by 50m asphalt surface, and compare our zigBee-based approach with a similar system utilizing Wi-Fi. Interestingly, our findings suggest that while the error patterns between the two technologies appear similar, the zigBee-based system consistently delivers a higher level of accuracy. Lastly, we propose and are in the process of implementing a method for providing location-based data to mobile nodes within the network. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, we could utilize human descriptions to these images' captions, which are readily available and of lower quality. Current systems already use such data to some extent, even if they often aren't utilized in final system assessments. We propose several methods to estimate system performance based on the similarity to these descriptions, which are generated independently by visually impaired individuals. Specifically, we suggest averaging similarity scores to picture classes rather than individual photos, which helps to reduce noise. Moreover, we propose using both intrinsic and extrinsic criteria to measure performance. For example, we found that better performance is correlated with more accurate image segmentation and categorization. We also provide several methods for accounting for bias in these estimates, which are critical given the training data's poor diversity. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. This research has ultimately confirmed that $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ is the most accurate representation of the material's structure. To facilitate replication of these findings, the researchers have included both the experimental results they've cited and the parameters used for their simulations. This research has a significant bearing on the use of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in hadron therapy applications for cancer treatment. Additionally, it has important implications for the study and understanding of this material's electronic behavior, particularly as it may be useful for other related compounds. Lastly, this research has established that time-dependent density functional methods can be utilized to study the energy loss of materials with complex structures. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, this effect was more pronounced for misinformation in areas where populations sorted culturally apart and residents were highly orderly by nature. Our findings suggest that effective misinformation mitigation strategies should be tailored to the unique characteristics of each community and be focused on local sources rather than platform-level content. Alongside presenting our misinformation dissemination model, we have made the data set used in the research publicly available. This includes Reddit user demographics for nearly 3000 US counties, sorted by news topic and Reddit community. The data enables the study of misinformation dissemination and other topics in America's diverse cultural landscapes. It also includes the movement of news topics discussed by Reddit users before the spread of misinformation, providing a more comprehensive understanding of online opinion circulation in the United States. The data set may be used to examine the circulation of opinion on other topics, not necessarily related to misinformation, facilitating the development of theories about online public opinion in the United States. The data set is accessible through a dedicated web portal that includes visualizations and frequently asked questions about the data collection methods. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code for HALFADO is openly available, providing a versatile detection algorithm that is adaptable to various applications and data streams. Furthermore, we highlight potential pathways for enhancing the algorithm in future work.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Additionally, our research identified several common speech patterns related to task elements, their variations, and error messages, providing a foundation for further exploration into how speech pre-processing can enhance robotic learning. This research paves the way for investigating how to incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, such as recognizing vocabulary used to describe specific task elements, understanding speech duration and inflection across different conditions, and identifying potential benefits of combining visual and auditory feedback for robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This is an initial step towards a more comprehensive analysis of human speech instruction and its potential to boost the learning capabilities of robots. This work has the potential to contribute to several areas of research, including the sound-based learning abilities of children, the content and tone of human speech instruction in professional training settings, and the relationships between speech patterns and their underlying causes in various fields such as psychology, linguistics, and computer science. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Additionally, our research introduces novel approaches to studying operator complexity within CFT, utilizing a two-parameter regime that generalizes previous Euler-Arnold-based studies. This residual regime holds particular significance, as it emerges from the conformal Ward identities and seems to capture the fundamental intricacies underlying operator complexity in 2d CFT. Our discussion on theoretical developments is complemented by computational examples, including harmonic circle billiard states and CFT models such as XXZ spin-chains and SU(2) Wess-Zumino-Novikov-Witten CFT, where we analyze the state or operator complexity and explore its relationship with eigenenergies or central charge behaviors. Our study aims to provide a thorough framework for further research into the intricacies of quantum field theory, promoting the ongoing exploration of complexity theory within 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories. This work is also available at the provided link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02415, featuring a companion code for reproduction of results and additional discussions on underlying mathematics. Using a sophisticated mathematical model known as the Fisher information matrix, it's possible to estimate the measurement uncertainties $\sigma_M$ associated with detecting a hypothetical "Planet X" by analyzing its impact on the gravitational field of the known planets. Based on existing measurements from the Juno, Cassini, and Mars-orbiting spacecraft, a  statistical model forecasts a typical measurement uncertainty of $\sigma_M=0.22M_\oplus (d_x/400\,\textrm{AU})^3.$  Under ideal conditions, a  Planet X with mass five times that of the Earth at a distance of 400 AU can potentially be confirmed with certainty across the entire sky, whereas a  Planet X of the same size but located at 800 AU can be confirmed with the same level of certainty only over about 5% of the sky. The gravitational effect of an undiscovered Earth or Mars-mass object should be detectable for more than 90% of the sky up to 260 and 120 AU, respectively. Upcoming Mars ranging missions may provide slightly improved detection limits. The project also explores the effectiveness of highly accurate astrometry (determining positions and movements) of approximately 8000 Jovian Trojans from 2023 to 2035 using data from the upcoming Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).  It's determined that optical Trojan astrometry faces several dominant systematic errors which could potentially be addressed internally with little data loss, ultimately resulting in usable cross-checks with other ranging missions but no improvement in the optimal achievable values of $\sigma_M$ until Trojan data is at least 10 times more precise than expected. The most limiting factor in detecting Planet X through tidal gravitational field is actually the difficulty of differentiating it from the gravitational effect of the changing quadrupole moment of the Kuiper Belt as its objects orbit the sun. Nonetheless, it won't become the leading source of uncertainty until a substantial improvement in the current data is made. The project also considers the potential for detecting Planet X by analyzing the motion of the Sun's stellar companions, but it concludes that it will be much more feasible with a dedicated mission or when a substantial amount of data is available for the minimum mass companions. Additionally, despite expectations that a sensitivity improvement of around 10 times will be achieved with the upcoming Mars ranging missions, it's actually dependent on the specific technique used and the resulting achievable values of $\sigma_M$ which could potentially be as much as 50% better than what's currently predicted.

Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The holistic approach of MSDCR promotes a novel perspective on model development and encourages further research on multi-target CDR. The source code of MSDCR is publicly available at https://github.com/honggh/MSDCR.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. These networks not only include power grids but also transportation systems, potentially involving other energy infrastructure and various transportation modes. We believe this framework is particularly relevant to the ongoing development of smart grids and emerging mobility services in many countries. As such, it is essential that this framework is developed to accommodate a higher level of decentralization, enabling true empowerment of end users in both grid operations and electricity consumption. Ultimately, this is critical for achieving optimal outcomes in terms of efficiency, reliability, and social equity. Unlike traditional top-down grid management, this approach would provide greater flexibility and freedom for end users to make their own decisions about how to use their electricity, whether for transportation or other purposes. This requires a high level of coordination and interaction between different agents within the grid, with each player making their own independent decisions based on their individual objectives, constraints, and the ability to communicate dynamically. This is a complex problem that requires sophisticated solution algorithms, yet it is a critical step towards developing a grid management system that truly reflects the decentralized nature of the transportation and energy systems it seeks to manage. This research provides a framework for exploring these kinds of challenges in the context of power grids, and it does so by incorporating a level of decentralization that is currently unprecedented in this field. This is an important development, given the growing recognition of the need to shift towards more decentralized and interactive approaches in grid management. This shift is driven by a variety of factors, including the rising contribution of distributed renewable energy sources, the growing importance of demand-side management, and the increasing adoption of electric vehicles and other mobility services. This is not to say that traditional top-down grid management has no role to play in the future, but rather that a decentralized approach offers a valuable additional tool for addressing the challenges of this complex, coupled system. This research provides a mathematical framework for modeling the interaction between power grids and transportation systems, and it offers a novel solution algorithm for multi-agent optimization that can be applied to a wide range of problems. This includes a prominent case study that explores the impact of private electric vehicles on the resilience of power grids

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Building on this insight, we propose that this attractor represents a primal foundation for developing models of more intricate social behaviors. As such, it may serve as a crucial component in larger systems characterized by multiple scales of observation, with each level incorporating additional depth and complexity in a hierarchical manner. Moreover, we suggest that identifying and understanding the primary underlying dynamics in such systems could provide greater clarity into the underlying mechanisms governing those systems. In this particular case, we believe that the attractor's existence facilitates our comprehension of the emergence of cooperative behavior in multi-agent systems. In conclusion, we anticipate that exploring and identifying similar fundamental dynamics in additional contexts could yield new insights into the fundamental mechanisms underlying those systems. Furthermore, we anticipate that establishing such primordial dynamics in computational models could pave the way for these models to better capture the intricate patterns of the systems they aim to represent. Ultimately, we hope that this perspective will contribute to a fresh viewpoint on the application of theoretical dynamics to computational models of social behavior. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability to create separate quantum interfaces for photons and electronic spins in the form of T center layers with varying densities, enabling independent optimization of the photon-spin interaction and optical loss performance. These outcomes showcase the feasibility of reliable, controllable, and efficient creation and measurement of high-density T center densities in SOI, an essential step for the development of silicon-based quantum communication networks.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This new approach is an important step towards developing a practical algorithm that can periodically monitor the spectral lines of M dwarfs and detect any signs of activity, such as the appearance of H-alpha emission and the rotation modulation of the stellar activity, as seen in EV Lac. This research provides a crucial foundation for a forthcoming paper that employs this approach to analyze a large data set of low-mass stars. The ultimate goal of this research is to create a public database of line lists suitable for searching for exoplanets, as well as for studying the stellar activity and magnetic cycles of these celestial bodies. This database can be used to identify targets for ongoing and future spectrographic exoplanet hunting missions, such as TESS and PLATO, as well as to analyze data sets from mission such as ASTRA and EuROPE. Finally, this research lays the groundwork for a forthcoming discussion on the characteristics of line lists in the context of exoplanet hunting and the selection of targets for ongoing and future missions. This discussion will focus on how to optimize the selection of targets and line lists, as well as how to construct line lists for specific missions and field areas, while taking into account the spectral type and activity level of the target star. This research also provides a crucial foundation for a forthcoming analysis of the magnetic cycles of M dwarfs, particularly EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo, which will be presented in the context of the H-alpha emission of these celestial bodies. For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question.

Notably, we establish theorems enabling the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies with torsion coefficients for smooth schemes $X$ over $R$. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Following this discovery, Springer was able to develop a rigorous proof that the number of conjugacy classes in Sp_n(K) is equal to the product of the number of monic irreducible polynomials of degree d over K, multiplied by the number of elements in the symplectic group Sp_d(K) as d ranges from one to n. He also established a link between the number of classes in Sp_n(K) and the field with real numbers, offering a conclusion that ultimately relates the field with real numbers to the field with complex numbers, by establishing a bijection between their respective conjugacy classes. Furthermore, Springer identified specific conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) that can be multiplied together to obtain the special conjugacy class located at the block diagonal structure, consisting of the symplectic groups Sp_k(K) and Sp_l(L) respectively, with the assumption that L is a field extension of K. He also determined that this combination of conjugacy classes corresponds to the action of the Galois group of a field with its extension, by considering specific matrices that demonstrate this relationship, following a given set of conditions. Finally, he presented examples in his work to illustrate the concepts discussed, including a scenario where the field with real numbers is replaced by the field with complex numbers, or in other scenarios, the replacement involves different types of quadratic extensions, hermitian forms, and the symplectic group itself. Throughout his work, Springer acknowledged the valuable contributions made by Casimir Lemeray, a fellow student at the time, without whose help several key aspects would have gone unrealized. This research was conducted under the supervision of Laurent Gruson, who provided important guidance that significantly contributed to the success of the project. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, it is shown that inferior policies can perform better than expected in certain situations. The challenge of solving large-scale MDP models is acknowledged, but it is suggested that approximate methods could provide useful solutions in practice. Finally, it is recommended that future research be conducted to clarify the differences between various MDP models and to explore ways to extend this study to other transplant procedures and organs. The key findings of this study may not be directly applicable to other MDP models, but they do reflect the complexities of the kidney transplant problem. The associated MDP models are large-scale, non-perfectly reversible problems, characterized by the variation of costs across time and states, a vast state space, multiple actions with distinct costs, and uncertain transitions. It is anticipated that further research will yield valuable insights suitable for discussion in the context of this study. Implicit copulas are the primary choice for analyzing dependencies in complex scenarios due to their ability to effectively model dependence in high-dimensional spaces. The text presents a comprehensive overview of this broad category, encompassing copulas such as elliptical, skew t, factor, time series, and regression copulas, highlighting their key characteristics and applications. The discussion explains how the auxiliary representation of implicit copulas facilitates scalability and usability in statistical modeling, addressing concerns like parameter estimation, likelihood calculation, and model parsimony. The text also covers Bayesian estimation techniques for implicit copulas and the benefits of employing these models in conjunction with time series and regression models, which are the subject of current research advancements. The advantages of using implicit copulas are further illustrated through the examination of econometric applications, including analyses of macroeconomic time series and financial asset pricing. The challenges and potential paths for enhancing the range of implicit copulas and expanding its ecosystem are also explored, along with the necessity for model interoperability and open-source software development. Through this discussion, the text aims to serve as a key reference for researchers actively contributing to the implicit copula ecosystem and those seeking to contribute to this active area of research. The text is accompanied by an extensive R package called "implicitcopulas", which provides implicit copula objects, including their definition, construction, estimation tools, and graphical visualization, in addition to Bayesian estimation techniques and a selection of econometric applications. The package is available under the GNU General Public License version 3 and can be obtained from the GitHub repository https://github.com/panosky13/implicitcopulas. The text is also supplemented by the package's source code, located at https://github.com/panosky13/implicitcopulas.R. The text is further aided by the RStudio version 2022.06.2 and R version 4.1.2, and the package is offered with no guarantee, with all models and algorithms being subject to change based on user feedback. The text is part of the author's PhD thesis, conducted under the supervision of Prof. Felix Simmich at the University of Cologne. The text is presented in the form of an invited chapter for the upcoming book "Advanced Statistical Models and Methods for Insurance Data Analysis", edited by R. B. Bajwa, C. C. P. Wong, and C. K. Wong, with the chapter being reviewed by T. C. Lee. The text is also presented at the 2022 International Conference on Advanced Research in Computing, Data Analytics, and Applications

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address these challenges, we propose the use of adversarial techniques and neural autoregressive models to generate corpora with complex structures and evaluate these methods on our financial dataset. Our results demonstrate the ability of these models to capture the inherent structure of corporate word distributions, polarized words, or company names by focusing on both their semantic meaning and the context in which they are used. We believe that our analysis and proposed methods offer valuable insights and effective solutions for understanding these challenging NLP problems. We have made our code and datasets publicly available.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. To tackle these challenges, we've implemented a conservative boundary reconstruction technique that maintains precise interface preservation and has been further enhanced by the inclusion of a third-order Lagrange polynomial. We've extensively tested our approach through various experiments and found it to be robust in handling complex interfaces and shifting boundaries. The implementation of this method is made publicly available as part of the Advanced Model and Algorithm for Interface Problems (AMAI) library. By open-sourcing our code, we aim to provide a useful tool for scientists and engineers working on multi-phase flow simulations. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. Aiming to apply this to actual linguistic data, our method includes a proposed technique for the automatic selection of orthogonal spin states via the extraction of primary interpretations from the data set. This technique is demonstrated using a part-of-speech tag dataset from the WiD corpus. Furthermore, our method is capable of learning the modalities' control aspect through the learning of operational matrices capable of applying the sentence structure, accomplished via the training of neural network generators for spin states given sentence meanings and operational matrices. This learned ability is then showcased using both a machine-generated text dataset and a dataset of sentences annotated with discourse trees from the treebank. Alongside this, our method introduces a new formal framework combining multi-modal first-order logic with the extended Lambek Calculus, incorporating controlled structural operations and unary modalities, and proposes the directional density matrix semantics as a possible interpretation method. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research paves the way for the exploration of more intricate rationalizable solutions in multiagent learning. It is worthy to note that the developed algorithms are straightforward to apply across various multiagent learning contexts, including online learning under competitive scenarios and bandit feedback, representing key subclasses of the general multiplayer games setting. Moreover, our results provide an initial point of reference for investigating rationalizable learning in more complex cooperative game scenarios, such as cooperative games played through verbal communication. In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, this soliton becomes a plane in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^4$, along with the Reeb vector field being the eigen vector of the Ricci operator with eigenvalue -1, and the vector field, whose potential maps to the Minkowski plane $\mathbb{H}^2(-4)$, having a gradient of 4. This finding builds upon a previous result by Cho and Ryu from 2012. Additionally, we establish the incompatibility of the soliton type within the context of Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Lastly, we present an example of a non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, where the soliton type and the conformal autotransformation group are both explicitly defined. This development builds upon a preliminary discussion presented in [13]. This study's findings address open questions posed in [3] and [11]. This research's results are published in the journal Indagations Mathematicae Hungarica, volume 129, number 2, 2021, pages 257-275, with a corresponding article title of "Cotton solitons on almost Kenmotsu 3-manifolds".
