Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we have developed an open-source framework that can automate the integration of theoretical predictions and data, enabling the evolution of PDFs and the generation of outputs compatible with popular PDF fitting codes. To ensure the reliability of this framework, extensive testing has been performed using a range of processes and datasets, and it is made available under an permissive license to facilitate its adoption by the research community. As a result of our efforts, we have been able to successfully fit EPSJPDF, and the code that accompanies this study includes instructions for potential users to adapt the framework to their own needs. As the field continues to evolve, with potential developments affecting the PDFs, we plan to continue updating our framework to address emerging challenges and facilitate further research. To that end, we welcome feedback and suggestions from researchers with an interest in this project. The code that underpins this study is available online at https://github.com/lhpc-group/XPDF-FIT, along with a comprehensive documentation that includes instructions for potential users and contributors. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence of these strategies, we aim to demonstrate their common effectiveness, ultimately involving the transformation of supersymmetric matrix integrals into related quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints. This equivalence is key to applying the superbosonization formula directly to derive double-sum representations of supersymmetric determinants. Consequently, we can obtain an alternative proof of the Witten-Determinant Formula for broad classes of non-Gaussian matrices. Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases. 
The results revealed a spin asymmetry value of 0.26, with a 95% confidence interval, 
which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44. 
This measurement's precision is expected to be enhanced with additional data.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Additionally, our analysis of the Knight shift supports the coexistence of multiple metallic states across all measured thicknesses. A comparison with LaCuO$_3$ reveals faster spin-lattice relaxation in LaNiO$_3$ despite both materials possessing similar correlation temperatures. A notable exception is seen at the Ni$^{3+}$ orbital by comparing LaNiO$_3$ and LaCuO$_3$ where the spin-lattice relaxation is significantly faster in LaNiO$_3$. A 91.5 MHz frequency increase in relaxation time was observed between the two materials. A theoretical model involving a multi-component metal state and SP-SC coupling has been proposed to reconcile our findings with previous reports on LaNiO$_3$. A detailed analysis involving the calculation of lattice relaxation contribution at the orbital for both LaNiO$_3$ and LaCuO$_3$ has been performed to further understand these observations. A discussion on the proposed theoretical model is presented and possible future directions for investigation are outlined. A summary of our main conclusions is provided and our study is placed within the broader context of the field. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our findings demonstrate significant 
improvements over baseline generators in terms of conversational quality and 
efficacy. Moreover, our dialogue generation framework is openly accessible for 
further development and refinement. In addition to our principal study, we 
examine two auxiliary problems involving listener-viewer relationships and explore 
the interplay between generative models in conversational scenarios. Our code 
repository is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/multitalk.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. As part of this work, we also present a mock galaxy catalogue created using MG-GLAM for the $f(R)$ gravity model and based on the Planck cosmological parameters, which will be made publicly available through the Halo Repository. This code is designed to be adaptable to other modified gravity models and can be accessed through a collaborative GitHub repository along with in-depth documentation. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. The framework's simplicity makes it an ideal solution for developers to create new CRDTs with consistency guidelines, enriching the domain of distributed systems technology. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. For example, around 30% of SNPs with the highest rank have a p-value of less than.05 and around 50% of the most re-ranked SNPs are in a strong linkage disequilibrium with an initially identified prominent signal. By examining re-ranked lists over time, we have observed that the relationship between genomic elements and associated SNPs is not always straightforward and can vary across different traits and cell types. For example, DNase-I hypersensitive sites that were once associated with platelet counts, but are no longer associated with SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within platelets, but are associated with a significant number of enriched regions within other cell types and are linked with a significant number of promoter elements or CPG islands that are targeted by various factors and are essential for the expression of essential genes in various cell types. Furthermore, we have identified specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with bowel disease and obesity related SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types such as macrophages and adipocytes and have observed that obesity related SNPs are linked with a significant number of promoter elements or CPG islands that are targeted by various factors and are essential for the expression of essential genes in various cell types. Our results demonstrate that a thorough examination of genomic elements can increase confidence in associations, shape our understanding of the role of genomic elements in influencing specific traits and pinpoint specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. We analyze the impact of acoustic waves on one-dimensional flows in general,
focusing particularly on massive stars experiencing outbursts exceeding the
Eddington limit. By leveraging approximate adiabatic invariants, we expand the
classical equal-area technique to include both integral and differential forms.
We model and simulate shock behavior within initially finite sinusoidal wave
trains, identifying distinct patterns for internal shocks, and both head and tail
shocks, and confirming that our predictions align with numerical simulations.
The findings reveal that our new expressions for shock heating rates provide a
more accurate account of the internal shock dynamics.
The solution also highlights the significant difference in wave energy preservation
at large radii between head and tail shocks, with a potential greater impact on
matter ejection. This distinction emphasizes the importance of waveforms in
shock evolution.
We also predict shock behavior to transition from weak to strong and utilize
this to estimate mass loss in scenarios involving rapid sound pulses and minor
central explosions. Additionally, we anticipate that in scenarios involving large
explosions or near-Eddington limits, where central shocks could become strong and
preserve more energy, our model may be applicable, and further justify the
need for multi-dimensional simulations of such scenarios. The new framework also
allows for a re-examination of potential shock wave mechanisms responsible for
the mass loss observed in massive stars. The study sets the stage for the
next-step analysis of how waves might interact with potential instabilities in
stars. The new expressions for shock heating rates, together with the equal-
area technique, now also enable the consideration of additional factors that
could influence shock behavior, such as radiation transport, electron inflation,
and heat advection, making it even more relevant to the transport of energy in
radiative stars. The new framework also opens up the possibility for a fresh
analysis of potential shock wave mechanisms responsible for the mass loss observed
in massive stars. The study sets the stage for the analysis of how waves might
interact with potential instabilities in stars, which could provide further
insights into the mass loss processes in this category of stars. The new
predictions for shock behavior in wave trains also raise the question as to how
these findings might impact the interpretation of spectral variations caused by
shocks in other types of stars. The new framework for shock analysis now
independently confirms the earlier suggested limit for weak and strong shocks in
super-ejectors, and further supports the potential for additional central

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview. Building on the foundational concepts established in the 1960s and 1970s by Auslander, Ringel, and others, the notes will explore the intersection of $\tau$-tilting and classical representation theory, covering topics such as the representation theory of hereditary algebras and Auslander-Reiten theory. Along the way, we will see how the precise language of $\tau$-tilting theory offers a fresh perspective on established results, in addition to showcasing the elegance and power of the theory itself. Although the notes are structured to be broadly accessible, we will inevitably encounter more advanced concepts and prove key results along the way to develop the necessary tools for our later discussions. These tools will include the definition of $\tau$-tilting theory itself and a comprehensive exploration of the category $\tau$ for a finite-dimensional algebra. As such, the notes may also serve as a concise guide for the established researcher looking to delve into the realm of $\tau$-tilting theory. As we explore the intricate relationships within the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras, we hope to convey the spirit of the field through its most influential contributors and most significant breakthroughs. Ultimately, our objective is to inspire further inquiry among the next generation of representation theorists and contribute to the ongoing evolution of the field. As such, we welcome feedback and prospective contributions from our audience in the form of comments and new developments. These notes are available under a creative commons license to facilitate maximum dissemination and to encourage the widest possible participation in the discussion. The corresponding author is particularly grateful to the editors of the Centre de Recerca Matem`atica for the opportunity to contribute to this volume and to the next generation of representation theorists for their enthusiasm and insights that have made this project so enjoyable. The author would also like to express their thanks to the University of Melbourne, the University of Oulu, the University of Osnabruck, the University of Oxford, the University of Oulu, the University of Sheffield, and the University of Tokyo for their support and hospitality during the research

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. It was also found that this technique raises the bar for Natural Language Generation models to achieve similar performance in conversations as human users do. Finally, the findings of the paper suggest that neural conversational agents prioritize repetition over variety in responses and offer several potential explanations for this preference. The code and data utilized in the study have been made freely available for use by other researchers.

Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for calculating efficiency and background probability and discuss the application 
of two techniques specifically density estimation using Gaussian processes and 
artificial neural networks. Although widely adopted in other contexts, these methods 
have not been heavily employed for amplitude analyses. The article also introduces 
new applications for these models, such as leveraging sidebands to determine the 
density of background in multiple dimensions, as well as more comprehensive density 
estimation utilizing artificial neural networks. Furthermore, the article highlights 
the importance of careful parameter tuning and statistical inference for model 
hyperparameters in such cases. By leveraging high-level programming languages like 
Python's Pandas and scikit-learn, these techniques can be efficiently implemented 
even for complex decays analyses. Through concrete examples drawn from previous 
research, the article demonstrates the usefulness of these techniques in resolving 
the challenge of instrumental influences in hadron decay studies. Finally, the 
article encourages further innovation in this area by highlighting potential 
extensions to these methods.

Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. The code and dataset are available for download at:  https://github.com/aiwolf/ibail. The code for the calibration methods tested is based on the PyTorch framework. The codes used for the experiments have been openly shared on GitHub at https://github.com/aiwolf/ibail to facilitate replication and further research. Despite the relatively limited size of the datasets employed in this research, the findings provide valuable insights into the challenges of incremental learning from imbalanced datasets and propose calibration methods as a viable solution. Nevertheless, large-scale dataset evaluation is necessary for this research, particularly given the rapid growth of new datasets in the field of computer vision. In the future, we plan to conduct extensive testing on larger datasets to validate the findings presented here. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has yielded impressive outcomes when tested against certain heart imaging data sets, although real-world medical imaging presents unique challenges due to variations in image quality stemming from the specific medical imaging technology used and individual differences in heart conditions. For this research, we first evaluated how accurate models become when they are trained with publicly available, labeled data sets (specifically, the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC) set) and then tested against CMR data obtained from TOF patients, or vice versa. Then, we sought to find out whether these models could deliver comparable results when tested against a broader data set with more diverse cases. Ultimately, this indicates that models developed for rare conditions such as TOF should be validated against a diverse range of new cases before being utilized in real-world applications. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. The code has been made available on the public GitHub repository https://github.com/CYH888/Easy-FPN-Implementation.

SS-WDS' ability to leverage large amounts of unsupervised data also allows it to achieve superior performance when compared to traditional supervised WSD methods. Our research implies that large-scale transformer-based models have a great potential to address the WSD challenge. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. The results show that this self-balancing feature allows for a two-fold increase in operating frequency range without compromise, and can also mitigate the negative effects of motion sickness on entanglement rate by as much as three orders of magnitude, depending on the chain length. Finally, we show that this type of gate can be an essential component in a large-scale quantum computer, specifically in the simulation of the Heisenberg spin chain model, and that, when executed on a chain of thirty-three ions, this model can exhibit quantum coherence for time durations exceeding one hundred seconds, a milestone in quantum computation. The proposed gate protocol can be applied to various configurations of trapped ions and offers a robust solution for addressing the effects of motion on quantum gate operations. The publicly available Qgate Toolbox now includes an implementation of this gate protocol. In a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer, typically used for calibrating a gyroscope's angular momentum, a notable spectral shift around anomalies occurs. This spectral shift within the rotating gyroscope can be understood in relation to the longitudinal Doppler shift experienced by the opposing light beams in the Sagnac interferometer. A mathematical analysis, taking into account the gyroscope's rotation and the geometry of the Sagnac setup, yields a frequency shift formula that demonstrates the effect in question. Furthermore, this approach results in an expression that connects the spectral shift to the Earth's gravitational potential, making the gyroscope's rotation-based sensitivity related to its angular momentum. This relationship is confirmed through experimental rotation of the gyroscope at varying speeds around its axis, demonstrating the predicted shift in several spectral lines of a laser source. The observed spectral shift around rotation anomalies is confirmed through additional experiments using a gyroscope subjected to oscillatory rotational motion, in both air and a vacuum. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes. This work also offers connections to prior studies on skew Dyck paths and recursive evaluation of preorders in trees. Altogether, new results are derived for the number of deepest nodes, both conditioned and unconditioned, providing an analysis of its convergence across various tree ensembles. This work is further illustrated by numerical data and theoretical insights derived from generating functions, offering a framework that can be applied to similar problems involving tree structures. Finally, several open questions in this area are posed for future investigation.

To further validate these results, a statistical analysis was performed to account for potential sources of random variation, which confirmed the observed outcomes. In addition, a detailed examination of individual ballot head and tail errors revealed that iOCR exhibits a substantial advantage in capturing tabulation data, especially in cases with limited spell-checking. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study also demonstrates that the resonant frequency-based attack can target multiple rooms simultaneously. Furthermore, we were able to successfully test this technique at a fully functional FDA-approved NPR located within a biomedical facility. Our research offers several measures that could mitigate this type of attack. Additionally, we have developed an automated tool that is capable of identifying the resonant frequencies specific to individual DPSs, as well as determining the frequency of malfunctions caused by the music. Our study's resonance-based attack is a novel type of vulnerability that is applicable to a broad range of sensitive facilities that rely on similar safety-critical systems. Our research suggests that this type of attack may have implications that are relevant to other types of sensors that are subject to similar frequency manipulation attacks. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. As a result, there is an urgent need for further research in this area, to better understand the interplay between storage units' risk avoidance and price volatility in future power grids. Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In order to address the issue of class imbalance, we developed Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward yet scalable AL algorithm capable of selecting more evenly balanced data samples for annotation. Consequently, BASE outperforms random sampling consistently. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. 

In conclusion, our findings highlight the challenges associated with evaluating AL algorithms on small datasets and introduce BASE as a scalable, effective AL algorithm capable of selecting evenly balanced data samples for annotation. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. Notably, this phenomenon is observed exclusively within a narrow threshold of critical thickness. Any significant deviation from this parameter results in poor edge state quality due to the presence of doped channels or substantial bulk resistance from the hole reservoir. In order to trigger the anticipated resistance oscillations, a neutral non-filling condition must be satisfied. This condition is key to understanding the behavior of large-sized samples. Our study reveals the limitations and special conditions necessary for the appearance of quantized resistance related to helical states at the neutral point, and suggests that this phenomenon is highly sensitive to variations in bulk charge inversion or hole reservoir resistance in response to changes in electric field or doping. As such, it may be difficult to control the required neutral condition in actual device applications, necessitating a reevaluation of the prospects for useful device development based on this phenomenon.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, an incremental rollout strategy for the power allocation step was found to be highly effective. Unlike other coexistence optimization strategies, our method doesn't require centralized control or complex numerical solutions, making it suitable for real-time implementation.

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. The code and dataset of our research are made available at https://github.com/AJRobson/HiXray. The introduction of HiXray, along with innovative techniques like LIM, is anticipated to accelerate innovation in prohibited item detection and contribute to advanced security inspection technology. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Additionally, $J_n^T$ is shown to correspond to a colored Jones polynomial for bonds in any thickened surface, yielding an extension of the original colored Jones polynomial. Through this framework, we examine the volume conjecture for various biperiodic links. To further explore its properties, we present two constructions for $J_n^T$, including a pseudo-operator invariant and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Moreover, we demonstrate $J_n^T$ corresponds to a colored Jones polynomial for bonds on any thickened surface, providing an extension of the original colored Jones polynomial. Finally, we discuss the implications of this framework for the volume conjecture in biperiodic links.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. The proposed framework consists of three key components, namely schema linking, column selection, and value filling, with code available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/Zero-SQL-zh.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. This work aims to provide a comprehensive overview of graph-based learning in relation to privacy, examining various formulations of differential privacy on graphs, related challenges and promising applications, also discussing open research questions in this domain. This work is part of our recent publication in the 2021 IEEE Conference on Computational Intelligence and Security. In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems. The results showed that our approach successfully detected sensitive failures in the system, and the associated road patterns were highly varied, covering many potential failure scenarios with minimal duplication. Furthermore, we observed that faster search methods, while effective in identifying key findings, missed certain critical cases, emphasizing the value of thorough, slower searches in uncovering more exotic failures. Consequently, we recommend employing a combination of both slow and fast searches to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of the system's vulnerabilities. Additionally, we developed a demonstration to illustrate the consequences of adjusting control points, creating new challenging driving conditions, and implementing the search methodologies. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. We build a modern, versatile dataset called CMS (Music Captioning Dataset) consisting of 5,000 captioned playlists, which serves as both a dataset for captioning and retrieval tasks. Each captioned playlist contains a brief description (approximately 2 sentences) and is supported by an audio track (typically 10 minutes long). To further the field of music captioning, we develop and evaluate a range of models including sequence-to-sequence, disk-based, and retrieval-based strategies. Our experiments highlight the challenges and limitations of music captioning, which are characterized by the limited contextual information within audio tracks and the significant gaps between text descriptions and audio content. To bridge this gap, it is crucial to incorporate domain-specific features that capture subtle musical elements and their corresponding semantic meanings. Consequently, the development of custom music-labeled datasets and deliberate design choices can yield promising outcomes in music captioning. Notably, our best-performing model employs a combination of audio content analysis and neural language features, which achieves remarkable results on the CMS dataset and outperforms baseline models that are trained on public music classification datasets. Additionally, our research demonstrates the importance of retaining the contextual context within audio tracks to ensure accurate music captioning. To facilitate future music captioning research, we make the CMS dataset and our associated models available for public access. This dataset not only enables music captioning but also offers potential applications in music retrieval, where searching for captions can lead to relevant audio tracks. This approach has the potential to give users more control over music recommendation and enable effective summary of recommended tracks. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. This new stochastic hydrodynamic framework provides a versatile tool for studying interacting Bose gases, and can be used to simulate both moderate- and long-duration phenomena. The linearized version of this method serves as an efficient alternative to Bogoliubov approximations, especially for scenarios where both a precise quantum treatment and a direct comparison with existing theories are desired. The development of this model also paves the way for developing new theories and methodologies, and could be extended to include the effects of external potentials or steady-state situations. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature indicative of an outer mode, a variant of PTMs. This theory offers an alternate explanation for the origin of PTMs and suggests that magnetic activity associated with ELMs could provide a diagnostic tool for understanding the behavior of turbulent filaments in the edge plasma. Furthermore, this could also shed light on the characteristics of PTMs, which are closely linked to current within these fragile plasma regions. Lastly, this framework hopes to contribute to a greater comprehension of the relationship between turbulent edge plasma and the magnetic field, as well as the potential for PTMs to serve as a plasma thermometer based on their formation temperature being equal to the filament temperature. This study was conducted using data from the JET tokamak but is relevant to a broader context applicable to other devices like ASAS and WEST. Finally, it is proposed that in-order to further this research, global turbulence simulations such as the one employed here should be refined to incorporate a better understanding of plasma turbulence obtained from local models such as ELISS. This in turn could lead to greater insight into the underlying causes of the turbulent filmaments themselves. This study was conducted in accordance with the JET data policy, which permits the free sharing of data, and as such the authors invite feedback and suggestions from other researchers in the field. This research has yet to be reviewed by a journal for publication.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Furthermore, our research indicates that in scenarios where the LOS link strength is higher than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$, the IRS-provided virtual link exhibits negligible improvement in target parameter estimation. Consequently, the optimal implementation of IRS technology in radar systems is contingent upon the relative strength of the LOS link. Additional findings include the optimal allocation of IRS elements to the virtual link for target parameter estimation and the potential for enhanced unambiguous target motion detection. Given the potential of IRS technology to overcome obstructions and the diversity gains it offers, along with the relatively low complexity of its implementation, it is reasonable to anticipate that the integration of IRS technology into radar systems will yield substantial outcomes. Nonetheless, further research is needed to fully explore the capabilities and limitations of IRS technology within radar systems. The methodologies and findings presented in this paper provide a foundation for such ongoing research. The framework introduced also offers a starting point for examining other scenarios, including the integration of multiple IRS surfaces, where the focus would shift to optimizing target parameter estimation in scenarios involving multiple virtual links. The theoretical basis laid out in this paper may also be applied to investigate the effectiveness of IRS technology within other wireless communication systems. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults. The proposed evaluation framework has been made available online to facilitate the comparative evaluation of new fuzzers.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. To further validate our proposal, we also analyzed the NMC's performance on the CoRe 50 dataset and explored its extensions, including the use of multiple class prototypes and boundary adjustment. Our findings have significant implications for the study of continual learning, suggesting that the complex designs prevalent in deep continual learning research may be unnecessary when the foundation is a high-quality representation model. This work has been accepted for publication in the 2022 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR).

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Our study shows that in comparison to standard 5-fold CV, the j-k CV method yields substantial improvements in model performance. Furthermore, in settings with limited labels, the approach proves particularly effective at adjusting parameters in low-labeled settings, as evident from the notable improvements achieved. All code and models have been made publicly available to facilitate further research. Moreover, our study's code incorporates additional enhancements, such as the utilization of distributed computing, a specially designed metric calculator, and a user-friendly configuration file. In summary, our study presents reduced variance j-k fold CV as the definitive method for effective parameter adjustment, encompassing a code framework that is transparent, adaptable, efficient and openly accessible. This code framework is designed to provide a straightforward platform that is easy to use for machine learning model parameter adjustment, encompassing techniques like stochastic gradient descent and Bayesian methods, in both low- and high-labeled settings. In addition, this code framework is intended to be a starting point for machine learning model research, encompassing nature language processing, computer vision and biology. Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a suitable path to achieving magnetic analogs of twisted
superfluid and supersolid phases previously found in ultracold atomic condensates
trapped in optical lattices. Employing a cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory,
we prove that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions are responsible for stabilizing
these phases within a magnetic framework, whereas in ultracold atomic systems,
the required mechanism involves the pair hopping process. Moreover, we reveal
that the DMI strength at which these twisted phases are achieved is sensitive to
the strength of the interlayer interactions which can be adjusted through the
application of external pressure or interlayer shearing force. Additionally, we
show that DMI can be precisely manipulated by incorporating circularly
polarized light into the system. Our findings will provide valuable direction
for researchers in the experimental search for twisted superfluid and supersolid
phases in quantum magnets.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. Furthermore, since the probability of detection varies significantly across different recoil angle and velocity distribution combinations, our simulation suggests that limiting the selection to narrower ranges of laboratory energy E_R or corresponding narrower ranges of nucleon recoil velocity v_R would better align with the natural parameters of the problem. Ultimately, this would result in more robust, less correlated quantities that are less sensitive to velocity distribution characteristics in certain E_R ranges. We also provide event rate predictions for our research scenario at existing and planned experiments with WIMP-sensitive detectors, incorporating a variety of different detector materials and operating temperatures. These predictions take into account the velocity distribution of nuclei within these experiments and provide event rate forecasts for narrow ranges of laboratory energy or corresponding recoil velocities, which can be utilized in comparisons with future experimental findings. By doing so, these forecasts are meant to contribute to more informed discussions among experimental researchers and theoretical model developers. In addition, we propose using two specific quantities to evaluate the likelihood of our proposed research parameters being consistent with the data collected in each individual experiment: the normalized event rate relative to the total WIMP halo velocity distribution, and the event rate in each specific E_R range relative to the average event rate across the entire WIMP halo velocity distribution. These ratios are intended to provide a clear and unambiguous understanding of the correlation between different E_R ranges and the incident velocity characteristics of the detected WIMP-scattered nuclei. As such, they are crucial for accurately interpreting future experimental findings in this context. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous. Collective findings highlight the capability of ICCBFs to mitigate vulnerabilities in systems and the potential for their extension to real-world implementations. Moreover, the discussion on challenges and future directions in the field is also presented.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. Furthermore, our solution ensures fast scalability, with approximately 500 milliseconds required to process a single sample, and is compatible with existing MPC infrastructure. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This particular work will present various scenarios, both simple and complex, utilizing binary population synthesis, and will also introduce a new, simplified CE scheme that is based on the principles of these scenarios, with the aim of enhancing the accuracy of predictions for the end states of these CEs, and to facilitate easier integration with future multiple star CE scenarios. This new scheme will be incorporated into the binary star evolution component of the forthcoming version of the SEPS code, a next-generation binary and multiple star evolution code that is being developed to explore the complex behaviors of these systems. This new scheme will be particularly useful in predicting the outcomes of CEs in multiple star systems, which will be discussed in greater detail in the accompanying paper. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Our simulation results indicate the capability of discovering the HEFT dimensionless coefficient $c_S$ in the entire accessible parameter space at both colliders, while the discovery of the HEFT coefficient $c_T$ depends on the collider energy and the cut criteria for jet momenta, with $c_T$ detectable at 1 TeV but only with stricter jet momentum cuts at 3 TeV. The ability to distinguish the two leading coefficients may also be within reach at the two planned experiments with various combinations of cut settings. Finally, we demonstrate that the expected limits on the two leading SMEFT coefficients at the two colliders will surpass the current Tevatron and LHC searches by several orders of magnitude, with the precise predictions strongly depending on the correction scale and the choice of variable used to set limits. The capability of distinguishing the two leading SMEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders appears less clear, with the expected limits strongly influenced by the choice of renormalization scheme for the wave function mixing parameter $\rho$ and thus requiring further study. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. As a result, BoAnon is an highly effective BO framework capable of accelerating the discovery of high-performance computer system configurations. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  Our proposed framework, along with the associated datasets and a detailed tutorial, is now available for public access on GitHub, along with the paper that is being presented at the Extended Demos and Industry Tracks of the 17th International Conference on Semantic Systems.
