By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory. In operation, the prototype will receive raw data from the instrument, refine the data to optimal quality, and deposit the results in the archive. This prototype is now integrated into the Keck Data Reduction System software framework and prepares the instrument for scientific operations. Once Liger is commissioned, this prototype will become the basis for the actual Data Reduction System. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. Additionally, the composition of the oscillatory pattern can provide insights into the behavior of the model as parameters change. Finally, the analysis is applied to the original ecosystem model, and the relevant parameters are connected to biologically meaningful quantities, offering a clearer understanding of the model's dynamics and the nature of the singular point where the model's behavior transitions from MMOs to equilibrium movement. This analysis is also compatible with the methodology proposed by Kuehn and first implemented in the context of the model studied here. However, the focus on the model and its dynamics allows for the most valuable contributions to be the identification of the separating surface and its implications for predicting population shifts in the ecosystem. The results highlight the significance of distinguishing between inner and outer trajectories in the analysis of the model's behavior. The study concludes with the suggestion that further research is needed to fully comprehend the consequences of trajectories crossing the separating surface in the model. The work laid out in this paper provides a foundation for a broader investigation into the role of chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations in the Earth's system and other complex systems. The proposed approach can be used as an early warning system to detect impending population shifts in the ecosystem. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This implies that bulge formation is responsible for the missing downflow in the face of ascending galaxy mergers and star formation rates in the mass-star formation rate plane. The additional insight provided by this study also sheds light on the construction history of massive galaxy bulges, suggesting they were formed through a combination of magnetic disk star formation and major mergers. The extensive bulge assemblies present in massive galaxies have since been reinforced by minor interactions and gravitational interactions. The accompanying cosmic rays in these massive galaxies have also played a significant role in shaping their high-energy magnetic field. The next level of observational evidence on this topic will offer valuable new perspectives on the relationship between magnetic fields and the creation and evolution of massive galaxy bulges. The findings of this study also provide a crucial new perspective on the typical bulge morphology

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The evaluation shows that, subject to precise fence placement, a significant portion of compiled C programs can be verified and optimized in this context. Additionally, we highlight several notable safety properties that could be verified using our method. The proposed framework and verification techniques are complementary to existing fence verification strategies and may be integrated into systems that rely on cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade. The code for the algorithms and protocols discussed in this paper is available online at our research repository.

In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. It's also established that this Freiman's 3k-4 theorem holds when the underlying field is controlled, specifically when the integers in A and B lie within the range [-N, N] for some positive N. Furthermore, we derive a more general result known as an 'almost Freiman' theorem. Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(B^{H}+f)$, particularly proving that if the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ exceeds $Hd$, then its density function is square-integrable, or if $A$'s Hausdorff dimension surpasses $Hd$, then its density function admits a continuous version, thus providing a result already mentioned. Further, the situation where $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a non-empty interior $A$ is equivalent to $f$ being $\alpha$-H\"older continuous with a specific index $\alpha$, thereby generalizing previous results. Finally, a counterexample is provided to show that the condition of $f$'s $\alpha$-H\"older continuity is not necessary if the measure of $A$ is zero. This counterexample is based on a specific construction involving a stationary process, and involves further findings regarding the relationship between the spectrum of the transition operator and the $\alpha$-H\"older class, which may be worthy of further investigation in future research. This counterexample's analysis also yields an interesting open question. This work is motivated by and contributes to a broader study of fractional Brownian motion's images under non-differentiable functions, and also explores related topics in the context of self-similar processes, fractional processes, and function theory. This research is accompanied by a list of open problems and questions in these areas. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/Sabra-vrd. Our work provides an effective solution to the VRD false positive issue and offers actionable insights for future research. Visualizing the predicted relationships, we release VizBEV, a interactive dataset viewer enabling easy visualization and diagnosis of prediction results. Moreover, we introduce a new metric, BEV Accuracy, for assessing VRD predictions by analyzing the 3D bounding box in bird's eye view perspective. A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Conversely, we arrive at an existing conclusion about compelled multifactor authentication, as well as our assessment regarding hash functions, which merely reaffirms the existing doctrine set by the case of United States v. McClure. Lastly, we offer an original contribution to the ongoing debate about compelled decryption in the context of end-to-end encrypted platforms. Our framework enables a forced evaluation of the/effectiveness of such measures, leading to the conclusion that compelled decryption, in the context of end-to-end encryption, entails yielding any possible evidence along with the means to derive it. Consequently, this implies that compelled decryption amounts to compelled production of evidence, thereby aligning with the doctrine established in the case of Fisher v. US. Our study offers a fresh perspective on the longstanding debate between the government and encrypted platform operators, as well as advocates for the adoption of widely accepted cryptographic standards, specifically focusing on the compelled actability of encryption technologies. Ultimately, we believe that our framework can serve as a starting point for a unified theory addressing the complex issue of compelled actability in the context of modern cryptography. We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Alongside this, our study introduces new perspectives on the long-standing debate on physicalism versus effective theory in the analysis of complex systems and suggests that future generalizations may be achieved through a combination of operational descriptions and mathematical theories. Additionally, our framework raises important questions about the nature of abstraction in complex systems and how it relates to the inherent multiscale properties of these systems. As such, our research offers a theoretical foundation for investigating the complex interactions within nonlinear dynamical systems and sets the stage for empirical exploration of this science. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol was proposed, using less entanglement than previously known protocols. This proposed protocol has an entanglement cost of $16$, which is improved upon the best known entanglement cost for local distinguishability without the need for entanglement. This research therefore not only answers several open questions, but also provides new insights and a higher entanglement-assisted local distinguishability threshold for systems of three and four parties. Furthermore, several UPBs of larger sizes were constructed in this research, providing more opportunities to examine the relationship between UPBs and strong quantum nonlocality in systems of higher dimensions. This could lead to a deeper understanding of the properties of UPBs and their relationship with strong quantum nonlocality. This research therefore opens up several possible lines of inquiry, such as constructing UPBs of minimal size in systems of higher dimensions, or determining the strong quantum nonlocality of existing UPBs. Both of these possible lines of inquiry could lead to a deeper understanding of the relationship between UPBs and strong quantum nonlocality. This understanding could provide new insights into the properties of UPBs, as well as the phenomenon of strong quantum nonlocality itself. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As a result, the producer thread's performance, responsible for the generation of binary DAGs, is no longer constrained by the consumer thread's ability to process them, thereby achieving a significant gain of approximately one order of magnitude in program speed. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. One additional key benefit is the generation of diverse and structured information that can be useful for other NLP tasks. We also introduce a novel evaluation dataset where triads are intentionally created to test the ability of models to manage complex structural knowledge. We hope this evaluation dataset will serve as a starting point for future research aimed at assessing a model's capacity to manage knowledge graphs. This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. The article compares their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits, as well as how rescaled fractional kernels relate to inhomogeneous fractional boundary value problems. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. The proposed framework also offers potential applications beyond panoramic imaging, including uses in vision systems powered by rotating mobile platforms and multi-view reconstruction from rotating cameras with unknown vertical alignment. The code and data used in the experiments are available online at this link https://github.com/ahmadzaidee/SimplifiedPanographicStitching. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference (CVPR) in 2023. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. As a testament to its flexibility, our model has already prompted related theoretical work that could give rise to a family of related models, influencing our understanding of basal ganglia cortex function. In addition, this model has been made freely accessible via specialized software for neuroscience research. In conclusion, we believe this novel Parkinson's disease computational model, developed from marmoset brain data, represents a significant step towards uncovering the disease's complex pathophysiology and can become a benchmark for evaluating future brain circuit models. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. This outflow in turn appears to be directed towards the supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center, enhancing the merger-driven accretion of gas and potentially boosting the growth of supermassive black holes over a merger cycle. This effect is likely enhanced by an increase in active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas due to the collision of galaxies mergers, specifically a type known as major mergers, where the difference in mass between the two galaxies is 10 times as much as the mass of our sun over a broad spectrum from major to ultra mergers. This effect is likely an important driver of the growth of supermassive black holes, predicting a relationship between the outflow of gas and the accumulation of mass at a given stage of merger, a trend that is likely influenced by the interaction between active supermassive black holes and the outflow of gas due to mergers. This relationship is likely modified by the mass of the galaxy and its central supermassive black hole, a factor that is likely influenced by the galaxy's stellar mass, a feature that needs to be clarified by more observations.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. In particular, it is shown that this new method outperforms the traditional multivariate multiquadric method over a range of data sets. As a significant added benefit, the components of the new interpolation function can be differentiated analytically, which is a key advantage in applications such as nonlinear optimization and partial differential equations where this capability is essential. Moreover, our implementation is computationally efficient, requiring essentially the same amount of computational work as the original Wu-Schaback scheme. Consequently, this new interpolation method can be used as a highly effective alternative to the multiquadric method and is particularly well-suited for use in nonlinear problems where derivative information is required. In such cases, it provides a more accurate approximation with a smoother shape, especially in regions where data is available, without increasing the computational cost. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. The model's performance is compared to other state-of-the-art sub-filter models under various conditions, revealing that in situations where the model includes additional sub-filter modelling, it produces comparable results. Nevertheless, the significance of introducing specific multi-fluid model formulations in future high-resolution models is highlighted, especially where further research is needed to fully understand the implications of model assumptions at those scale levels. The presented model serves as a starting point for exploring the potential of multi-fluid models in addressing convection simulation challenges within high-resolution weather and climate models. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. An
interesting observation emerged when we adapted the model to classify the sentiment not
only at the tweet level but also at the user level, using only the training data from a small
sample of users. We explored both manual and automatic methods for selecting emotional
tweets and discovered that using the BERT model, which is easily accessible via the Bert-API,
yielded better results than previous approaches. Finally, we applied this sentiment analysis
to a large dataset of positively checked Twitter content, also known as "verified" users.
We discovered that many users with positive verification also post positive content,
while users with negative verification content go largely unrecognized due to the limited
availability of negatively worded tweets. Additionally, we identified a correlation between
users who post emotional content and those who are followed by many users. Finally, we
believe that this project's methods and findings will serve as a foundation for more
advanced research in public sentiment analysis.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our study demonstrates that the shadow radius can be an useful thermal entropy indicator for understanding phase transition physics in black holes. Ultimately, we derive a new equation that relates the shadow radius to effective pressure and entropy in both coexistence phases. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The code
and data generated by our approaches are made publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/role-constrained-dialogue.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida. The results showed that the simulated method's rankings aligned with the conventional method's rankings in 94% of cases, using data from the Florida strawberry industry. The study further demonstrated that the disease pressure impact, initially undetected by conventional methods, significantly influenced the efficacy of fungus management practices, revealing a 13% increase in the understanding of yield losses and a 11% increase in profit losses attributable to disease pressure after incorporating this approach. The simulated method provided statistically meaningful results with as few as 20 observations per trial, a significant improvement over the conventional method's requirement of around 100-150 observations. To facilitate replication and further exploration of this approach, the code is available for review and modification. Ultimately, this method enables farmers to make informed decisions about pesticide efficacy using a limited number of observations, thereby helping to optimize fungus management practices.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for certain graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete. Specifically, we prove a graph G has a 2-strong shortest path cover if and only if it is 2-link forest-free, and provide an NP-hard polynomial-time approximation algorithm for this problem. We analyze the performance of this algorithm, showing it achieves a cover of size O(k^2 * log(n)) for any k-hops cover of the same graph, where n is the number of vertices. We also examine specific graphs, including showing a 2-hops cover is equal to a 2-link cover for series-parallel graphs, and provide a 2-hops cover of size 3 for outerplanar graphs and 4 for planar graphs. Finally, we discuss the problem of finding the smallest k-hops cover, and provide lower bounds for certain graphs, including an lower bound of 4 for tree graphs when k=2. This research provides an extensive examination of the k-hops strong shortest path cover problem, including both general theory and specific graph analysis. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. Our research introduces a novel application of decision boundary analysis in knowledge distillation and offers efficient solutions for black-box distillation. This could have broader implications for situations where access to the internal workings of a network is necessary to improve its performance.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more. The approach allows an analytical construction of submodules, previously found through Ademola's approach, and enables the generation of new submodules. Furthermore, this method lays the groundwork for constructing lattices of submodules of modules without composition multiplicities, given their subfactor structure, offering potential implications for understanding representation theory of Lie superalgebras. The method is illustrated by constructing the lattice of submodules of $M(2,2)$, and the sublattices of $M(3,2)$. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. A chordal graph that contains a strong geodetic subset may contain a minimum strong geodetic vertex subset of size two, which can be determined in linear time. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. The source code is available at https://github.com-google/trail. Despite the various pros of imitating human demonstrations, the same imitation techniques can be dangerous when trained on problematic examples. We argue that utilizing suboptimal paths from other agents as data may be viewed as a form of data detoxification, helping to prevent the learning of undesirable behaviors from unhealthy expert data. The methods explored in this study are closer to offline reinforcement learning than traditional imitation learning, yet they share many similarities with those techniques. These approaches can be seen as a starting point for offline reinforcement learning methods that leverage expert examples more efficiently by initially utilizing non-expert data to inform the action space. The action space then needs to be dynamically updated with the help of online expert demonstrations. This study provides a foundation for offline imitation learning, enhancing the learning process by leveraging suboptimal trajectories and promoting more energy-based models that efficiently utilize various datasets. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. This suggests that PAC codes have considerable potential as efficient low-complexity alternatives to polar codes for error-correction applications with high information rates and limited side information at the transmitter. This could be particularly relevant for many modern communication systems that require high throughput and low latency.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement. A tolerance to sub-optimal actions, enabled by a policy which penalizes errors, represented a complementary technique that yielded another 0.7 BLEU points gain, as our results show. A major advantage of our approach lies in enhancing translation quality without necessitating a vast vocabulary, thus making our method highly compatible with other NMT models. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. In contrast to traditional approaches relying on fiducial markers, our method eliminates the need for physical preparation, instead using a camera alone to calculate end-effector position and orientation directly from real-world data. A key benefit of this approach is that it allows for the calibration of end effectors with complex shapes, such as those with surface cavities, by providing a more accurate way to estimate keypoints in such situations. Moreover, our method can easily adapt to different objects and end effectors by simply inputting new real-world data, making it an ideal solution for various applications involving a wide range of customizable end effectors and where, as an example, medical procedures require frequent adaptation of instruments for different patients. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Additionally, the relationship between continuous QFS-spaces and finite separating maps is explored, leading to the construction of specific types of QFS-space retracts. Lastly, the mutation of QFS-spaces within the context of upper power spaces is demonstrated. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. This result implies that there exists a deterministic algorithm with a time complexity of O(n^2) for solving V's word problem, where n represents the number of digits in the input, rather than the input's total size as previously understood. Additionally, we demonstrate that the context of equality in this relationship is necessary by showing that the word problem for a variant of V, often referred to as V^1, can be solved using a context-free algorithm. This finding indicates that the higher-order structure of V's word problem arises from a higher-order sequence rather than from a more complex context-free sequence. This new insight offers an entirely distinct perspective on the underlying syntactic properties of V's word problem and may provide a useful framework for further research. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a
u$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team constructed a binary catalog of around 2,700 candidates through the analysis of their light curves, radial velocity fitting, the extraction of binarity parameters from medium-resolution spectra, and cross-referencing it with the $Gaia$ EDR3 binary catalog. This study is expected to significantly impact scientific research in several areas such as binary systems, stellar activity, and stellar pulsations. Additionally, the LAMOST research team discovered several unusual objects including two candidates for white dwarf binaries, around 500 binary candidates around small-body candidates, and around 200 binary candidates around neutron stars candidates. The LAMOST research team also provided radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, binary catalog, and stellar masses, all of which are useful resources for follow-up observations and further research. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Furthermore, we identified potential issues with the correctness of MongoDB's transaction protocol in certain scenarios. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of MongoDB's transactional protocols and their consistency guarantees, and are relevant to other systems that may utilize similar protocols. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. As the Parker Solar Probe continues to draw closer to the sun, its instruments will be able to measure even more precise details of the solar wind's composition and behavior, providing a better understanding of how the sun's magnetic field and plasma interact to shape the solar wind's characteristics. Eventually, missions close as far as 15 times the solar radius will allow for the study of how the solar wind's structure and energy distributions change as a result of the sun's changing activity and variability. As for the four approaches studied in this research, the solar wind energy distributions showed distinct patterns related to how close the solar plasma was initially produced, with the energy distributions being highest at about 1.2 times the solar radius from the solar center, and displaying characteristics of falling according to a specific power law as you move further out. It is also worth noting that since the solar wind could reach such high temperatures despite being composed of mostly electrons with very little contribution from protons or other elements, it is likely that the energy distributions of the electrons themselves play a major role in determining the overall structure and behavior of the solar wind. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  Additionally, our results demonstrate that higher pressure can recover the magnetic order at 10K, albeit with increased magnitude, yet only once pressure drops below 8GPa.  We propose a multi-structural model to explain these occurrences, where different layers respond differently to pressure, leading to distinct structural and magnetic states across various pressure and temperature conditions.  Our study highlights the intricate relationship between pressure-induced structural changes and magnetic properties in BFTO, a notable example of a mixed-phase system exhibiting complex spin behavior.  This work also underscores the value of combining structural and magnetic measurements to explore intricate systems under high pressure conditions.  Further research is required to fully grasp the fundamental mechanisms underlying these phenomena.  This work offers a unique perspective on the intricate relationship between pressure-induced structural changes and magnetic properties in BFTO, a notable example of a mixed-phase system exhibiting complex spin behavior, and highlights the importance of combining structural and magnetic measurements to explore intricate systems under high pressure conditions, also suggesting that a multi-structural model is necessary to explain such complex phenomena.  This study also indicates that pressure can trigger diverse structural adaptations, local structure alterations and complex magnetic ordering across distinct layers within multi-structural compounds.  This work provides a starting point for further research on the interaction between layer-dependent structural changes and magnetic properties in complex systems experiencing multi-structural transitions under high pressure conditions. The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation. The resulting model explains the presence of rings, the growth of planetary components, and may help clarify the spacing between planetary systems. This could be due to large-scale instability in protoplanetary disks, leading to planetary core formation in specific locations. The increased conductivity in these regions makes it difficult for secondary dust formations to grow, resulting in isolated planetary systems until the first generation stars are formed. The model also predicts that planetary systems should contain multiple cores, as the primary process of their formation is efficient and repeated. The first observations of multi-planetary systems support this prediction, making the viscous ring-instability a key component in the development of planetary systems. The model requires further validation through direct observations of protoplanetary disks and the development of more refined simulations. The potential for future experiments and the model's predictions for its implications in the field are also discussed. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. Our research extends the application of DSGD to real-world scenarios and provides DR-DSGD as an open source code on GitHub. This code is optimized for the PyTorch framework and suitable for multi-GPU training. Our research and code offer useful insights and solutions for the challenging problem of distributionally robust learning in decentralized networks. They are available online at https://github.com/huang123456/DR-DSGD. We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of measuring the pressure has not been fully acknowledged in the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk phase-transition scenario. Our paper provides the fundamental principles of the hard-disk model, defines the concept of pressure and presents new, unbiased methods of estimating it. Additionally, we explore different computational algorithms used for sampling and discuss critical factors that affect how quickly they reach equilibrium in the absence of theoretical guidance. Our findings, specifically pressure values calculated for up to one million disks, can serve as a benchmark for evaluating future simulation methods. Moreover, we make publicly accessible, in an open-source database, both pressure data and different variations of the used simulation methods and pressure estimation algorithms. This initiative is intended to promote collaboration and contribute to establishing common standards for validating new simulation techniques. Furthermore, we offer numerical evidence that supports the prediction made over half a century ago by Fermi, showing that the equation of state for the hard-disk model can be accurately described by a continued-fraction expression. However, we also demonstrate that this equation fails to predict the pressure effectively at high densities, instead indicating a singularity at $\rho \approx 0.7888\pm 0.0004$ $\rho$ units per $\sqrt{\pi}$. This result was reached independently of any specific transition scenario discussion and provides a precise estimate of the density at which the singularity occurs. Over time, the hard-disk model has evolved from a standalone problem to a platform that contributes to a deeper understanding of more complex systems, such as the hard-sphere model and fluids. Consequently, resolving the mystery of the hard-disk model can be viewed as a significant milestone in the broader quest to uncover the underlying principles of statistical mechanics. Finally, we highlight the significance of achieving independent physical insight, free from theoretical predictions, by relying on unbiased methods of computing physical properties from numerical data. This approach is essential for addressing the fundamental challenges posed by the hard-disk model. Lastly, we outline potential areas for collaborating with theoretical physicists, researchers from the machine-learning community, and other numerical physicists by further exploring the principles underlying equilibrium and non-equilibrium states of the hard-disk system

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our research reveals the Forsage network's structural characteristics, including the continuous growth of users despite a fixed supply of investment opportunities, the development of user rankings, and the existence of reward mechanisms for top participants. By demonstrating Forsage's similarities to other well-known pyramid schemes, our research provides valuable insights into the underlying dynamics that drive and sustain these types of scams. Additionally, our research identifies several features that are commonly found in other hidden pyramid schemes, which could be utilized in the development of predictive models to detect unauthorized multi-level marketing systems disguised as legitimate businesses. By combining our in-depth analysis of Forsage with existing research on other hidden pyramid schemes, we propose an framework for classifying and presenting data on these complex systems. Finally, our research for Forsage serves as a model that is applicable to any other self-sustaining blockchain-based multi-level marketing system, and we encourage the open exchange of data to facilitate further study in this area. Through this research, we aim to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the difficulties of regulating cryptocurrency-based multi-level marketing systems and the hidden pyramid schemes that frequently go undetected. By examining the underlying dynamics of these schemes, we seek to provide valuable insights that can be utilized in the development of predictive models used to identify unauthorized systems disguised as legitimate businesses. Due to the visibility of its transactions, Forsage offers a unique opportunity for an empirical analysis of a pyramid scheme that has already been implemented on a large scale. By combining promotional content with complex transaction data, our study explores the intricate workings of Forsage, its impact on users, and its evolution

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs alongside the primary contributions of heavy-quarks in hard-scattering processes. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions as mass dependent entities. Our study provides detailed NNLL$'$-resummation order analysis (combining NNLL evolution with NNLO boundary conditions) to fully comprehend the primary and secondary quark-mass influences for $q_T$ and $\mathcal T$ across all pertinent scale relationships. Notably, in case of the $q_T$ distribution, distinct rapidity divergences arise, leading to an intricate understanding of rapidity evolution features, paving the way for precise quark-mass measurements at LHC in a ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra at low $q_T$, critical for determining the precision mass of the $W$ boson. Our research offers a framework for a thorough investigation of other exclusive observable behaviors in hadron-collider processes. To facilitate further theoretical and experimental research, we provide a detailed analysis along with numerical predictions for various differential distributions in Drell-Yan process at LHC and future hadron colliders. The associated code is made publicly available for the benefit of the particle physics community. The study highlighted in this paper will form a crucial foundation for our proposed framework to address primary and secondary quark-mass dependencies in other exclusive differential spectra at hadron colliders. The code is hosted at the GitHub repository https://github.com/rahulghosh/DY-EXINC for public access and community contributions. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We further establish that this compensation issue arises from the use of incomplete Wannier sets in the TB models. Consequently, we recommend utilizing the dipole-based model over the velocity-based model, especially when modeling the linear and non-linear optical responses of insulating systems. The techniques developed here provide a benchmark for assessing the accuracy of TB models and will help simulate optical properties of materials reliably. The methods discussed can be applied to a broad range of materials, including those with multiple Wannier bands, by using the formula derived to compensate for the incomplete Wannier sets.
