A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored. Additionally, the sensitivity of the quantum yield in a steady-state condition is proposed as a potential basis for understanding the precision of optical homodyne measurements in protein-based systems. Lastly, potential applications for this concept in complex light-sensitive systems are presented. A comparison is also made between the quantum yields of rhodopsin and channelrhodopsin. A scenario is also presented in which the system reaches a steady-state quantum yield of zero, and the sensitivity of the quantum yield to changes in intensity in this condition is less than optimal due to coherent effects. A comparison is also made between the quantum yields of forward and reverse reactions. The reaction time for forward and reverse directions is found to be similar, whereas the quantum yields for these directions exhibit a 10-fold difference. A potential explanation for this disparity, involving differences in initial conditions and nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing, is proposed. A further analysis in a microscopic picture shows that the primary source of chaos in this system arises from the nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing, and that the Lyapunov time for this system is on the order of 0.1 fs. A discussion is also presented on the relationship between this chaos and coherent effects that occur over a much longer time scale (10 ps). It is proposed that the steady-state quantum yield could serve as an indicator for judging the degree of chaos in complex light-sensitive systems. Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.

predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Furthermore, our findings suggest that Graph Neural
Networks excel in processes characterized by isolated event clusters. In contrast
with existing research, our results show that demonstration scores for prediction
accuracy are unreliable and can be misleading. Finally, our work incites the
development of more advanced deep learning models for flexible use in process
prediction and the availability of provenance datasets with substantial event
quantities. These datasets are essential for thoroughly understanding how deep
learning models behave in complex processes. The implemented models, data sets

completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization

cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified

embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The technique also improves the diversity of generated sentences as measured by inverse BLEU score. Our results show that sentence representations learned through sparse coding can improve the performance of subsequent processing modules in down-stream applications like machine reading. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdw/SparseGAN. We have also included additional figures and experimental results in the appendix, which is accessible at https://hjdw.github.io/SparseGAN/. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Our study utilized radio-telemetry and capture data from mountain lions in Colorado to demonstrate these methods' effectiveness. In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings. Moreover, we provide a $2k$-approximation algorithm for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem under the scenario of unit costs. Our techniques involve a novel combinatorial construct known as the Minimum Edge-Dominating Steiner Forest (MEDSF) problem. Through the development of a $8\sqrt{3k}$-approximation MEDSF algorithm, we are able to establish our 4$\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem. We also investigate the MEDSF problem in its own right, as it may be of independent interest. Additionally, we discuss upper and lower limits for the MEDSF problem through both general and near-optimal worst-case analyses. Our research implies that a sublinear-in-k approximation for Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths has been achieved for the first time ever. Our work on the MEDSF problem may serve as a foundation for further research and potential extensions to other edge-intersecting problems. Our design for the F-vortex object, a key component involved in our MEDSF algorithm, may also provide novel insights and contribute to the development of innovative solutions for other Steiner tree-related problems. As for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, we determine the lower limit for this problem to be at least $2k-1$, as this is also the case for its edge-unweighted variant. As such, our $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm represents a significant breakthrough in the field when costs are unity-based. The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding dynamic processes on complex networks, particularly near critical transitions. This study tackles this issue by measuring nodal activity to quantify localization in networks undergoing dynamic changes. The proposed method is widely applicable and can be employed with theoretical models, simulated data, and real-world observations. The researchers analyze spreading processes on various networks, demonstrating that nodal activity can display intricate patterns depending on the network's architecture. The findings indicate that localized and widespread patterns are not mutually exclusive features in a spreading process. Additionally, the prevalence of an epidemic near a critical transition is influenced by the delocalized component of the network. Furthermore, different critical exponents can coexist with similar localization patterns. The study also reveals a more intricate behavior in quenched networks, influenced by the type of activation and degree exponent. The work sets the stage for future investigations of localized activity in network processes. The method for quantifying localization is made available as a computational tool to facilitate comparison across different processes, networks, and research studies. The framework for assessing localization is versatile and can be adapted for use with other dynamic processes that exhibit temporal evolution in network systems. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. By publishing these methods, we intend to facilitate new methodological developments that make the most of broadcast location data, to explore previously unaddressed research questions in football. Ultimately, our approach will contribute to a richer understanding of the complex strategies involved in football, and the role that individual players play within them.

Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the analysis of the detected text features. Our research indicates that our relationship-determination technique performs better than rule-based methods and confirms that visual features play a key role in achieving high accuracy in these situations. Our technology has the potential to make significant contributions to the analysis of historical documents. Our results show substantial improvements over prior research and set a new standard for the identification of both types of text and their relationships in deteriorated forms. Our technique has been made available openly to promote further development in this field. It has also been applied to real-world scenarios, such as the analysis of old financial documents. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/hip_rssm.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles. Lastly, we discuss the scalability of these results to non-Hermitian matrices. We've established that non-Hermitian matrices following the GUE, GUE perturbed by a GSE, and GSE matrices all satisfy asymptotic conditional freeness. We've also shown that the asymptotic conditional freeness of these matrices results in the distribution of their outlier eigenvalues conforming to a specific quadratic relationship. This discovery, along with an analytical formula for calculating probabilities within the phase transition region, allows us to provide an improved explanation for the known sharpness of the BBP phase transition. Additionally, we've established the analogous quadratic relationship and quadratic monotonicity for non-Hermitian Jordan normal matrices, and have utilized this understanding to provide an analytical description of the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues in certain classes of large non-Hermitian matrices. Lastly, we've established the direct relationship between asymptotic conditional freeness and the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues in non-Hermitean matrix models. This has led us to derive new results for the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues in various non-Hermitian matrix models, including a class of complex random matrix models that include both GUE and GSE. We've established an direct relationship between asymptotic conditional freeness and the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues in non-Hermitian matrix models. This has led us to derive new results for the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues in various non-Hermitian matrix models, including a class of complex random matrix models

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods. Additionally, we provide a suite of artificial networks that can be utilized for testing and normalized data on multiple commonly employed measurement methods. This research paves the way for a thorough assessment of the methods and facilitates further experimentation by offering both method evaluation and a suite of artificial networks that can be employed for testing. The code is available at: https://github.com/alexfoster/StructuralPolarization. The data is available at: https://github.com/alexfoster/StructuralPolarizationData. The standards used for evaluation are available at: https://github.com/alexfoster/StructuralPolarizationCriteria. The standards used for evaluation are also briefly outlined in the main text.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. If the Einstein operator is understood as the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator, then the Einstein equations are equivalent to the Einstein field equations with a constant Ricci scalar, implying that general relativity's Einstein field equations are the first order of the Bianchi equations. This work also explores other operators related to the Cauchy stress operator, including the Einstein operator, and discusses both its significance in the context of general relativity, as well as the relationship between these operators and the Bianchi differential module. The discussion extends to possible applications of the Einstein operator in theories of gravity other than general relativity. The paper also analyzes the role of the Einstein operator in the context of the Einstein field equations, and the confusion surrounding it among renowned scientists. The relationship between the Einstein operator, the Cauchy stress operator, and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator is also examined. The paper's conclusions can be used in any theory of gravity in which the Einstein operator, defined as the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator, plays a key role. The paper's findings regarding the Einstein operator and the Bianchi differential module may also have implications for the development of new theories of gravity. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. Once changes have been made, the tool can display the modified code and the corresponding changes it has identified in a reliable and trustworthy graphical format. This environment and its associated tools can be integrated with industry-standard software development tools, including those used for editing code, detecting errors, and compiling programs. A prototype of this environment was implemented with a case study involving the verification and testing of an operating system kernel. The results showed that this approach can effectively verify and test the reliability of the kernel by finding and fixing mistakes in a relatively small number of attempts. Furthermore, this approach can be an efficient and trustworthy tool for verifying and testing the reliability of dependent software, including applications with safety and security concerns. These applications include flight control systems, medical devices, and security systems, among others. Verification and testing are activities that are central to the development of dependent software, and they should be integrated with other development activities in a collaborative approach. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5. The comprehensive evaluation includes a rigorous analysis of model performance along with an exploration of the effects of promoter length and network architecture on HyperPrompt's success. The code for HyperPrompt is openly available at https://github.com/chacza/HyperPrompt. Moreover, a supplementary documentation containing additional results and discussions can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03.39.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena. Furthermore, it paves the way for applying symmetry protection principles to other phenomena, such as momentum conservation, in this regime. Moreover, this study demonstrates the capability of cavity QED systems to exhibit symmetry-protected multi-quanta phenomena and facilitates the development of more complex quantum phases and collections of atoms. This finding also enhances the potential for exploiting protected quantum phenomena in these systems and offers a greater understanding of the transition from single-quanta to multi-quanta dynamics in the ultrastrong coupling regime. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. These characteristics make the algorithm versatile and effective across a wide spectrum of applications, including the distribution of degrees in sparse networks and the resolution of the leader election problem in a probabilistic model. The algorithm's conception involves the incorporation of threshold-based decisions into a suggested protocol, followed by an analysis of its behavior under uncertainty through the application of probabilistic methods. The executable code for the algorithm used n=13,500 in the research conducted by the authors is now publicly accessible online. The authors also present an implementation of the algorithm using Python's NetworkX library in association with the SciFEM-SCARF finite element solver for an elliptic partial differential equation. The authors' research was conducted with the support of funds from the European Research Council. The authors propose an innovative approach to address the challenge of estimating a sparse complex network's size, offering the algorithm's source code for broader exploration and development. The authors highlight the algorithm's decisive advantages of being uncomplicated, decentralized, and requiring minimal computational expenditure per round. The authors also showcase the algorithm's effectiveness in scenarios with an unspecified number of malicious nodes, specifically in networks with power law degree distributions, demonstrating its robustness in such environments. The authors present an intriguing idea of employing the algorithm as a prototype to solve other intricate network problems, such as determining the network's structural characteristics or selecting a leader node efficiently. The authors provide the source code for the algorithm used in their research, offering other researchers a chance to build on this concept or modify the code

This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term

The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic

intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

management software. The developers provide an example of the method's applicability

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The simplicity of this approach also enables a direct connection between the physical parameters of the spacetime and the conformal connections, leading to new insights into the properties of black holes surrounded by scalar fields. The simple formulation of this approach also enables the construction of approximate solutions for boundary value problems. The description of initial conditions is also provided in a new set of "physical gauge" charts, where the geometry and conformal connections can be represented in a particularly simple form. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through a series of numerical tests. The paper also presents a novel solution to the problem of defining physical parameters in black hole initial data, where the spacetime geometry is determined by a set of conserved charges rather than source terms in the Hamiltonian constraint. The traditional approach to solving the Hamiltonian constraint in numerical relativity involves decomposing the conformal factor into a sum of terms, with the coefficients determined by projecting the Hamiltonian constraint onto a set of basis functions. This method is notoriously difficult to converge, especially when solving for the conformal factor in the presence of matter configurations. In this work, we explore an alternative approach to solving the Hamiltonian constraint, where the conformal factor is instead determined by solving an algebraic equation derived from the Hamiltonian constraint. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As demonstrated with data across multiple user projects, this approach facilitates real-time data analysis to provide near-instant feedback to users and automate quality control, quality assessment, and data selection. This methodology also enables multi-instrument analysis by integrating data from diverse measurements, such as x-ray diffraction and spectroscopy, to solve complex problems. As shown with two case studies, this includes determining crystallography and surface chemistry. By integrating machine learning into beamline workflows, this work paves the way for enhanced data analysis, automated measurement refinement, and efficient data interpretation, all tailored for real-time use and actionable for users without machine learning expertise. This framework is also shareable and modifiable to cater for distinct applications and beamlines. As user facilities like NSLS-II are expected to adopt similar machine learning approaches across all experiments, this work serves as a model for integrating this technology into existing workflows. This approach can also be applied to other user facilities and potentially adapted for other automation and experimental techniques. As a result of this work, several machine learning models have been developed, contributed to open-source databases, and incorporated into Blueky, and are available at https://github.com/NSLS-II/Blueky-ML. This includes projects focused on crystallography, surface chemistry, thin film thickness, and spectroscopic analysis. This methodology is intended to facilitate collaboration and stimulate the development of additional machine learning models to further enhance these measurements and tackle novel challenges. As this work initiates a comprehensive machine learning for experimental development at user facilities, it is hoped that it will serve as a foundation for a code-to-data pipeline,

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio. A key finding indicates that a higher anisotropy results in higher frequency and growth rate, ultimately leading to a possible GAM frequency limitation. Despite the linear analysis, a possible scenario for GAM instability can arise when a specific bi-Maxwellian anisotropy is exceeded, which may intensify instability in nonlinear regimes. Moreover, this study provides growth rates and frequencies for bi-Maxwellian ions comparable to those found in research involving Maxwellian ions. A comparative examination is also conducted between linear gyrokinetic and algebraic gyrofluid theories for modes with high frequency and spatial modes with large spatial harmonics. A major discrepancy is discovered in locations with strong mode growth, namely the core region and areas with sharp gradient changes, indicating a limitation in algebraic gyrofluids when modeling unstable GAMs. A deeper investigation is needed into how this discrepancy relates to nonlinear GAM phenomena. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Moreover, our research offers a potential solution to overcome decoherence limitations in complex systems via the careful selection of Hamiltonian parameters. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. The writing is informed by previously unexamined archival material, particularly the van Rhijn Archives held at the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory, although also drawing on established literature and additional sources. The effective collaboration between the governing board and directors during this period, involving significant decisions that shaped the lab's path, is the central focus of this research. The eventual arrival of director Blaauw in 1957 marked a turning point for the lab, and his own career trajectory is placed within the broader context of the European aerospatial industry at the time. The ultimate outcome of their collaborative efforts led to the lab's emergence as the Kapteyn Institute, now an independent research institution within the University of Groningen, and also saw Blaauw become the first director of the European Southern Observatory in 1960 - both milestones occurring shortly after his tenure at the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory. The successful revival of the lab during this period laid the groundwork for its future growth, allowing it to become a prominent player in modern astronomy. The legacy of van Rhijn, however, remains more complicated to assess, with his contributions to the lab during his time as director existing in a state of tension with the challenges he faced. The available archival evidence does not present a clear enough picture to permit a definitive evaluation of his impact relative to the broader developments in astronomy during this period. The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.

The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
This groundbreaking approach offers a pathway for developing more precise damage detection methods and correcting existing limitations in conjunction with physical models.

We're exploring the possibility that there's a parallel between brain neurons and societal individuals, inquiring whether collective intelligence requires individual intellect and what specific forms of individual knowledge contribute to greater collective insight. By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications. Additionally, we propose that true collective wisdom arises when individual intellect is aligned with collective goals. However, our analysis also reveals that unintentionally sharing certain forms of knowledge can lead to destructive coexistence similar to the observed societal "arms races". Furthermore, we propose that synthetic systems capable of both individual and collective learning, in line with our proposed framework, would be capable of evading such deadly coexistence through observation of internal dynamics. In doing so, such systems would achieve a state of cooperative coexistence, analogous to the optimal policies derived from reinforcement learning. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. Moreover, the findings suggest that remote learning presents an opportunity to explore instructional methods previously inconceivable in traditional face-to-face classroom settings. Consequently, this research lays the groundwork for further investigations into the compelling questions that emerged from the analysis. By doing so, it can contribute to the advancement of inclusive educational technologies that promote learning excellence across all demographic spectrums. paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation

Ultimately, our findings underscore the capacity of our proposed logic to offer

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of using a non-invasive BCI approach with high resolution cortical readings to regain control over lower limb prosthetics in paraplegia. Nonetheless, a critical step would involve testing this methodology with actual patients equipped with prosthetic devices, enabling seamless interaction between the individual's neural signals and the prosthetic technology. Conclusion: Due to its precise level of resolution, a cortical-based BCI has displayed excellent performance in predicting walking states and step rates when subjects walk, run or talk with a load, providing a promising means to safely control modern lower-limb prosthetics and potentially address paraplegia's mobility challenges.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Implementing this method using Python, we've made the algorithm publicly accessible on GSocLib's repository for nested sampling and related uncertainty estimation. By providing NSPy, a Python module based on this algorithm, we've further made the following two new libraries accessible: APyProbability, which includes various probability distribution tools, and APyBayes, which offers Bayesian estimation tools, all seamlessly integrating with NSPy. By employing NSPy's uncertainty estimation, we've achieved notable improvements in two non-related benchmark problems. Due to its open-source nature, we encourage contributions and advancements on this algorithm. Additionally, we've released NSPy, APyProbability, and APyBayes under the liberal Apache 2.0 license, making them suitable for use in any project or scenario. The developed algorithm has significant potential to contribute to various biological and technological applications such as animal activity analysis, biomedical research, and video games, alongside potential uses in driver assistance systems and robotic interaction with living subjects. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Our simulations are further supported by periodic boundary conditions, where we present examples of topological phase phenomena in atomic and photonic systems consisting of multiple units of Su-Schrieffer-Heeger networks. This study provides a theoretical framework for understanding topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated disorders, which can be applied to atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. This research also offers a possible pathway for experimentally inducing topological Anderson insulating phases in atomic or photonic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models via binary disorders. Lastly, our findings propose that systems with correlated disorders can exhibit multi-level topological phase diagrams, giving rise to novel types of localization in real and momentum spaces. This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our decoder framework not only tolerates faulty measurements but also enables the learning of decoding strategies from raw data, overcoming previous limitations that required noise models to be incorporated numerically into the decoding process. To further enhance performance, we developed a method to train decoders in a way that simulates the effects of measurement errors during training, leading to improved results. This approach enabled the generation of decoders with superior average performance across various noise scenarios, outperforming conventionally trained and tested decoders by a significant margin. Finally, we successfully created decoders that could adapt to new noise models through retraining, showcasing the potential for a decoder that could be deployed with minimal prior knowledge of the system noise and then fine-tuned to perform optimally in various environments. This research provides a foundational framework that offers insights and innovative solutions to develop efficient surface code decoders, laying the groundwork for a crucial component in the development of large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality. The proposal offers a promising approach for making precise quantum measurements using realistic optical systems. The system under study is also compared with other applications of quantum metrology, offering possible solutions to its current limitations. The ability of this approach to continuously monitor and continuously provide information about the system's state through quantum feedback control is also the basis for further study and potential applications. The approach is also shown to exhibit superior precision when dealing with drifting optical cavities, a typical problem in optical resonators. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot reached 70% of the desired height in a single hop. However, larger foot sizes resulted in decreased efficiency due to the buildup of granular material underneath, leading to reduced hop heights. To move forward, this work suggests incorporating sensory feedback into force control systems when interacting with soft grounds, as well as advocating for the use of DEM-based RFT in analyzing the dynamics of legged robots engaging with spherical granular surfaces. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our research underscores the significance of advanced NLP models being able to accurately process negation without resorting to cumbersome workarounds and lays the groundwork for future research directed at overcoming the significant challenges posed by negation. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes. Lastly, the theoretical findings are confirmed through numerical simulations. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored. Our research utilized a dataset containing 5000 Twitter posts annotated with positive, negative, and neutral sentiments and demonstrated that the NLP pipeline consisting of Tokenization, Part-of-Speech Tagging, Named Entity Recognition, and Syntax Analysis significantly impacts the efficiency of machine learning models. Among the evaluated machine learning models including Stacked Linear Regression, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting, Gradient Boosting exhibited the highest accuracy at 80%. Furthermore, the incorporation of feature engineering using decision trees and the NLP pipeline resulted in a 14% enhancement in accuracy. Our research also explored context learning of the dataset based on sentiment using Word2Vec and proved that context learning of datasets with positive, negative, and neutral sentiments is distinct. Additionally, the incorporation of context learning based on sentiment into the pipeline led to a 24% improvement in accuracy. Our research provides valuable insights into the analysis of Twitter data, context learning of datasets, and the NLP pipeline, offering numerous opportunities for further exploration in this domain. Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of planar stripes and charge domains enabled alternative Josephson coupling theories. Our study finds the average intralayer interaction to be greater than interlayer coupling and comparable to condensation energy, ultimately yielding long-range phase order-driven superconductivity. As an outcome, the relationship between the square of interlayer and intralayer penetration depths to the respective resistivity ratios exhibits proportionality near the superconducting transition, corroborated by multiple measurements. The ratio of the longest Josephson coupling length to penetration depth defines the phase domain size, and is seen as the length scale separating magnetic and electrical properties in cuprates. The findings provide a theoretical basis for a new phenomenological framework that relates the superconducting state to resistance through self-consistent Josephson coupling and condensation energy. The proposed model is applicable to all cuprate superconductors, allowing for a unified discussion of the superconducting state across various materials. The study also includes a detailed analysis of the electron-doped cuprate Nd$_{0.85}$Pb$_{0.15}$Sr$_3$ScO$_5$ where the long-range phase order and superconductivity are mediated by Josephson coupling. The unique structure of this material prevents the onset of antiferromagnetism, allowing for a true competition between magnetism and superconductivity. Ultimately, our work suggests that long-range phase order and Josephson coupling play a critical role in the superconducting state found in all cuprate materials. The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  Our findings demonstrate that the sound velocity's conformal limit behavior depends on the phase transition's tension, while the adiabatic index remains relatively constant across different phase transitions.  This phenomenon could lead to new insights into the quark phase's nonperturbative nature and may offer a potential explanation for quark stars' possible massive nature.  Furthermore, this could introduce a novel marker for quark stars, potentially allowing the identification of these stars through the sound velocity's conformal behavior and subsequent phase transition analysis.  This research also highlights the importance of considering the hadron-quark phase transition's parameters in the context of neutron star phases.  Ultimately, our predictions for the sound velocity's conformal limit behavior and the adiabatic index's independence of density could be verified or rejected via high-precision measurements of neutron star sound velocity or through the detection of quark stars.  This knowledge could ultimately provide deeper understanding of the quark phase's nonperturbative properties and help distinguish between the various types of compact stars.  This research is also driven by the appearance of the new GW190814 pulsar, which has sparked debate over its nature, sitting ambiguously between the known population of high-field and low-field neutron stars.  Inspired by GW190814, we're exploring the fundamental properties of compact stars, including their sound velocity, adiabatic index, and potential quark phase transition, which could help shed light on the mysterious nature

The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. We then demonstrate that this restriction is NP-hard by showing a reduction from the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem. We also discuss how the computed lower bound can be utilized within the cutting plane method for solving the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We highlight that any feasible solution for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping can be represented as an integer partition of a specific set, defined as the set of weights computed for all possible anti Tai mappings. We conclude that armoring the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem with integer programming would yield an efficient algorithm for solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem by applying the cutting plane method. We also propose alternative approaches for solving the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem directly. Finally, we provide evidence that the computed lower bound can significantly outperform the currently available best-known upper bounds for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem when one tree is a path. We present several open questions related to the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem, including armoring the problem directly and determining whether a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping always exists between any two trees. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In these areas, particles with sizes between 0.1 mm to 1 fm exist in a steady-state condition, where development on one side balances settlement on the other. This outcome, in turn, affects the VSI's operations, suppressing it in areas around the midplane. As a result, a vast region in these disks is protected from VSI, allowing gases to maintain stability through thermal diffusion. This outcome may help explain the thin disks characterized by minimal settlement, where VSI is often observed. In these areas, additional energy sources, such as magnetic fields or external forces, might be necessary to stimulate dust development and facilitate further settlement. In conclusion, our research indicates that particle growth has a significant, often dominant role in VSI's operation within protoplanetary disks, leading to a complex interplay between gas, gas cooling, dust, and dust development that, in turn, affects how these disks evolve and develop. In this process, dust development and settlement may provide a key mechanism that regulates VSI's reach and, as a result, a major driver of protoplanetary disk evolution. In this research, we offer several predictions that can be tested by analyzes of various protoplanetary disks and offer a framework for exploring the intricate connections between gas, gas cooling, dust, and dust development within these systems. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This research has implications for the interpretation of Gaia's parallax measurements and may be applicable to other similar missions, such as the Space Astrometry Mission. To validate the effectiveness of these measurements in verifying the gravitational parameter $G$ might need reevaluation, potentially using the most accurate $\gamma$ determinations from individual stars. Finally, we suggest that raw data from Gaia and future similar missions should be preserved to take full advantage of evolving theoretical models and participate in $G$ validation with the most accurate approaches available at the time of analysis. 

This study's findings will help accurately interpret the results from these measurements and ensure the optimal use of such a valuable dataset. Additionally, it highlights the importance of thoroughly understanding the astrometric system's fundamental characteristics to effectively validate general relativity's predictions and explore its limitations. 

This work is now being expanded to examine the deviation of another post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\alpha_2$, which affects the gravitational influence on light's speed, which will have a distinct effect on the measurements discussed here. This research is also being used to evaluate the gravitational impact on the measurements expected from the PLATO mission, a forthcoming exoplanet mission, and will be the subject of a upcoming, separate study.

Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical-lattice potential and utilizes interaction forces with opposite signs to create an equilibrium where both solitons accelerate equally. Meanwhile, the total momentum remains conserved. Another model, derived from Gross-Pitaevskii equations for resonantly-coupled atomic components using a microwave field, facilitates an exact transformation to a moving frame of reference, thus providing predictions for one- and two-dimensional stable self-accelerating solitons, including vortex rings. The theoretical properties of these models can be experimentally realized using a suitable trap and optical-lattice potential, thus making them feasible for observation in actual BEC experiments. The theoretical properties predicted by these models may also contribute to a deeper understanding of collision forces in actual BEC experiments. The research described herein may also spark further theoretical investigations into the properties of binary BEC systems. The predicted self-accelerating solitons can offer a novel means of colliding solitons with varying collision forces, which may also provide new avenues for the manipulation of solitons in such systems.
