This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. SIMC 2.0's enhanced design provides enhanced privacy protection and improved efficiency for various ML models, including support for convolutional neural networks. By achieving significant performance gains without compromising privacy, SIMC 2.0 paves the way for the wider adoption of secure ML inference. Moreover, our proposal incorporates an innovative programming model and simple-to-use APIs that enable developers to incorporate SIMC 2.0 into various ML frameworks with minimal effort. As a result, our proposal requires only minor adjustments to standard ML framework code. As an example, the Kaldi framework experienced only a 5.3 percent performance degradation with our secure protocol. To facilitate easy adoption, we have made the source code and benchmark data available online. In conclusion, SIMC 2.0 represents a pivotal advancement in secure ML inference due to its superior efficiency, versatile application support, and the minimal performance degradation observed in our experiments. As such, it provides a robust foundation for the development of additional secure ML protocols and the protection of various data types, including outputs from other ML models, as illustrated by our private image recognition protocol. As a result, we believe that secure ML inference is now sufficiently efficient for real-world implementations. As such, we plan to build upon this success by exploring new applications for secure ML inference. As such, we invite researchers to join us in this endeavor and contribute their expertise and knowledge in this exciting and rapidly evolving field. Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. This method is versatile and applicable to various graph topologies, including rings and trees. Moreover, our results reveal that the algorithm's convergence rate accelerates linearly with the number of random walk steps until convergence. This phenomenon is analyzed both theoretically and numerically. Furthermore, our algorithm achieves greater convergence rates in scenarios with large statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets. With regard to communication costs, our algorithm reduces the communication required between nodes and the server by an order of magnitude compared to other random walk algorithms. This method is robust and applicable to a wide range of machine learning models, including linear regression, logistic regression, and neural networks. Our experimental results validate our proposed algorithm's effectiveness and efficiency in these contexts. This algorithm offers a viable solution to address the challenges posed by data distribution among nodes in Federated Learning applications. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. This concept is explored through analyses of previous studies, observations, and laboratory experiments. Furthermore, it is suggested that the recent discovery of large, persistent eddies in polar atmospheres may be akin to the self-sustaining patterns found in idealized models of mid-latitude jet turbulence. These findings are advocated through numerical simulations that replicate the large-scale characteristics of the winds without instability, confirming that the bi-stable idea can indeed hold across these two applicable contexts. Lastly, the interplay between wave turbulence and the geostrophic vortex is delineated as a bifurcation process that is responsive to changes in rotational velocity and vortex strength. Consequently, it is proposed that suitable models for bi-stable flows be developed through high-resolution simulations of rotating turbulent flows. This would enable a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms giving rise to the bi-stable conditions, followed subsequently by the development of closure models for the resulting inertial wave turbulence. By integrating these closure models with the vortex segment model, it is possible to obtain a unifying theoretical framework for both wave turbulence and the geostrophic vortex. This proposed framework also suggests that the vortex segment model, when coupled with closure models for wave turbulence, could be employed to develop forward-driven models for rotating turbulent flows. By doing so, it may be possible to simulate the evolution of the turbulent flows for extended periods of time, thus providing a deeper insight into the bi-stable concept and the cascading processes within rotating turbulent flows. Ultimately, it is anticipated that this proposed framework will contribute to a greater understanding of the mechanisms governing the bi-stable conditions in rotating turbulent flows, as well as the downscale energy cascades that give rise to the persistent geostrophic vortices. An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, it's also evident that a substantial proportion of those benefiting from treatment, around 30 percent, do not experience a lowered likelihood of returning to the justice system and may be viewed as a separate population.  Consequently, the existing data isn't sufficient to justify targeted intervention on this basis.  Instead, the data could be used to direct research towards better identifying these two distinct offender groups and the most effective treatments.  The research employs a method that minimizes potential biases and avoids relying on statistical techniques that assume a specific relationship between variables, providing results that can be viewed as an initial exploration of the data rather than a definitive conclusion.  It suggests that a more in-depth study is required to fully determine the relationship between court-ordered mental health treatment and future crime. To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. By establishing an operator $Q$ which facilitates this technique, we show that $Q$ is also surjective and its domain is equal to the kernel of $P$, when $M$ lacks compact components. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our best outcome, achieved by combining the alphabet transfer with coarse-to-fine training, resulted in a 16.3% WER decrease on a mobile speech dataset compared to the baseline. We also obtained comparable performance to the current best Czech ASR models but with minimal adjustments and without incorporating any additional techniques commonly employed in high-performance ASR systems. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/fajkw8/PrAgMR-TraFfEr.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This model also helps us understand a phenomenon we observed, where at certain speeds of expansion, the length of clusters actually increases instead of decreasing. This happens because the particles are reassembling quickly enough to catch up with the expanding surface, but only up to a certain point, because then the stresses become too great and the particles begin to break the bonds that hold them together, and the length of clusters then drops again. This pattern we see fits the framework of "stick-slip" dynamics, which is commonly observed in other systems that experience sudden breaks due to expanding stresses. This theory also provides us with a new way to look at other floating systems, such as lakes and oceans, where the breakdown of ice can be influenced by the competition between the same two speed factors. Ultimately, this study gives us a deeper understanding of the breakdown of material systems that are affected by the competition between different timescales. This understanding can help us develop new strategies for designing materials that are more resistant to breakdown. Additionally, this study also highlights the significance of interplay between different timescales in physical systems, which is a crucial aspect that needs to be considered in various applications, such as engineering and astronomy. This study is a further extension of previous research done on the same topic, where the same principles were observed in a different scenario, where the surface of support was being compressed instead of expanded. This study also includes new experimental data that was not a part of the earlier research. This study also includes new analysis and new insights that were not a part of the earlier research. This study is a significant contribution to the field because it sheds light on a less understood aspect of material breakdown, which is the effect of expanding or compressing surfaces on material failure

This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. We also discovered that k is equal to n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3. Interestingly, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 when d = 4, indicating that it grows sublinearly in n. Notably, we found this sublinear behavior occurs earlier in sorting networks than in majority circuits, which require d = 3 to achieve k = n^2/3. We propose a new construction of sorting networks with arity 2^⌊log2n⌋ + 1, which sorts n inputs with a depth of 3. We also established that any sorting network with depth d must have comparator arity at least n/(2^d). We conclude that the best possible sublinear lower bound on k occurs when d = 4, which may imply that deep circuits are inherently required for sorting networks. We believe this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties and behavior of sorting networks and comparators. It also paves the way for further exploration into the intricate relationships among k, n, and d, and the intricate inner workings of sorting networks and comparators. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code and model weights are available online.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy. This finding is expected to contribute significantly to a deeper understanding of the exotic ground state of GdInO3. This understanding may also be applicable to other materials sharing a similar 1/3-magnetization-plateau feature, such as HoInO3, ErInO3, and TmInO3. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we established that for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, this fairness condition holds in an even weaker form, known as one-good fairness. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets. The code for our method has been made freely available for use by other researchers.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Moreover, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with a larger dataset, thereby highlighting the method's immense potential as the dataset continues to expand in size and diversity. By making the code and model available on open-source platforms, we hope to stimulate further research and development in this area. This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. A optional extension to our research investigates how the inclusion of luck's impact on future job opportunities influences people's opinions on redistribution. This extension results in participants preferring a greater gap in starting jobs, but have little intention to act on this in employment markets where job success is largely determined by luck. This research's findings are timely, as they address the ongoing debate about the relative importance of luck and skill in determining worker outcomes and the effectiveness of various redistribution policies. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The comprehensive studies conducted on the widely-used MultiAgentSoftActorCritic (MASAC) framework reveal that our method not only delivers stronger performance but also effectively handles scenarios with substantial differences in player performance. Moreover, an exploration of the impact of varying dataset diversity levels on the SIT framework is also included. The code is openly accessible on the MultiAgent Learning GitHub repository. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Moreover, our analysis showcases the superiority of single-particle entanglement as a resource for quantum information processing tasks, notably the steering and robust generation of single-particle Bell diagonal states. Finally, our findings highlight the potential for single-particle entanglement to undertake a variety of non-local tasks superior to that of multi-particle entanglement, notably the steering and robust generation of single-particle Bell diagonal states.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. This prediction is distinct from other models that also follow Population III binary remnants and may serve as a clear signature for identifying nuclear star clusters through gravitational waves. Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold. Furthermore, models incorporating the Quantitative Index of Knowledge revealed that the value of new knowledge is influenced by a nonlinear path, where the benefit of new knowledge diminishes at higher levels of disorder. Ultimately, this study offers a universal framework (KQI) that can be applied across multiple disciplines, such as physics, biology, economics, and sociology, to measure the growth of scientific knowledge. By providing a detailed analysis of the complex citation networks between authors, this work uncovers novel insights into the complex evolution of scientific knowledge and offers both theoretical and practical tools for conducting similar studies across diverse disciplines. Additionally, the publicly accessible dataset employed in this research will serve as a foundation for exploring new aspects of scientific knowledge evolution. It is crucial to acknowledge the self-organization principles underlying the development of scientific knowledge, where the value of new knowledge is influenced by a nonlinear path, where the benefit of new knowledge diminishes at higher levels of disorder. It is also evident that new knowledge is accelerated by the massive growth of literature, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold. It is hoped that this study will stimulate conversations about the evolution of scientific knowledge and encourage both theoretical and practical investigations into this intricate topic. It is also proposed that this index could be utilized in evaluations for scientific awards, such as the Nobel Prizes, where the winners are selected based on citation counts, but also take into consideration the Quantitative Index of Knowledge across their body of work. It is also contemplated that this index could be applied to various other complex networks and eventually even societal knowledge evolution. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical basis for developing secure, dual hop OFDM communication systems that can adapt to changing connectivity scenarios. Simulation results are promising and indicate that our proposed methods can offer substantial security gains over conventional adaptive transmission techniques. Nonetheless, we acknowledge that several scenarios, particularly those with multiple users and relays, require further investigation to yield more comprehensive insights. As such, we hope this study will serve as a foundational framework for future research in this domain. Conclusion - This research offers a theoretical framework for developing secure, adaptive communication systems using dual hop OFDM technology. As noted in the findings section, more analysis is needed for certain scenarios, particularly those involving multiple users and relays. Future work can build upon this study by exploring other optimization techniques and considering additional performance metrics. Additionally, investigating new detection algorithms and signal processing methods can further enhance the efficacy of these systems. As such, we invite researchers to contribute their approaches and share their experiences in this exciting field of research. Thank you.

On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the U(1) case, can be validated by testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. Our exploratory examination reveals that the Charge Convexity Conjecture is upheld in each instance examined, yet we have not discerned the underlying reason for this behavior from the perspective of conformal field theory. On the other hand, in theories where the convexity of a charge under a global U(1) symmetry is known to hold, such as in Yang-Mills theory and certain versions of the weak gravity conjecture, the relationship between the convexity of a charge and the weak gravity conjecture remains to be clarified. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The study also provides the model to the research community and future policy applications by highlighting its flexibility to explore various ancillary services and market designs. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency. Additionally, our study highlights the importance of treating experimental triggers and reconstruction procedures naturally within the matrix element calculation through the use of generator-level information. Consequently, we were able to retain up to $90\%$ of the uncut signal background, thereby reducing the need for additional tight kinematic cuts to enhance signal significance. Finally, our approach enables the exploration of new cut strategies based on distinguishing variables that arise from the matrix element calculation, along with the integration of machine learning tools to further enhance the separation between signal and background. This method enables us to establish the connection between local complete intersection varieties and their characteristic-p properties. Additionally, we explore the application of our method to the study of semi-parametric components in positive characteristic and the analysis of the properties of varieties defined over finite fields. By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware. As such, we anticipate that this framework will be a valuable tool for analyzing the trade-offs involved in the physical realization of quantum error correction.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. The major benefits of our approach include its versatility in handling various fracture types, compatibility with nonconforming meshes, and the capability to model fractural flow within mass-precribed boundaries. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Lastly, our findings are further illustrated by numerical experiments. Reply to comments from the editor and additional related theoretical analysis are also included. Our research offers an in-depth understanding of the Burer-Monteiro factorization and suggests it can help uncover implicit structures in complex matrix optimization problems.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios

mechanisms of medium-sized nucleus collisions. Lastly, our study reveals that

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The proposed framework is readily applicable to various dataset correction scenarios. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. A tentative proposal is made to amend the model by integrating a diffusion component based on Santiago's temperature gradients, yet further research is needed to validate this approach. A brief analysis is also conducted to assess the potential implications of modifying the model to reflect the unique characteristics of Santiago's infrastructure and social landscape. This study suggests that a model replicating the city's rioting patterns could provide valuable insights into the underlying dynamics driving the spread of unrest and informing policy decisions in a similar urban context. However, significant methodological limitations and the challenges of validating the model in a new context also need to be considered. A possible direction for future work in this area is outlined. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. With a dust correction similar to that of H$\alpha$, this line has a higher sensitivity to massive star formation and could provide a more accurate star formation rate if dust properties are known. However, we also find that dust extinction has a limited impact on this line relative to other rest-frame near-infrared lines, which could make it less useful for measuring star formation rates in dusty galaxies. Still, this line is important for understanding the stellar populations within 0.5 kpc of the galaxy's center through line strength or by comparing it to predictions from the model, which could potentially be used to constrain the dust content's impact on a greater scale. 

This study is part of the DEEP-GRISM3-Survey-as-a-Science-Project, which uses the WFC3 on the Hubble Space Telescope to conduct a comprehensive near-infrared spectroscopic survey of distant galaxy populations, and this analysis is based on data from one of the first observational programs. The data analyzed in this study were obtained from an exposure of 20,876 seconds to a single field, which was collected between October 2017 and April 2018, and this study is a preliminary exploration of the potential of the Brackett-$\gamma$ line to contribute to the interpretation of WFC3 near-infrared spectroscopy data.

This specific boundary overlaps with another critical boundary that involves nonnegative polynomials and is characterized by polynomials that become zero at at least one point. Our focus lies on a separate part of the boundary that involves positive polynomials and we have already successfully identified the complete description for some specific cases with low degrees in a small number of variables. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus inherent constraints, and indirect ones. We examine the effects of each set on the possible deviation of neutrino behavior from expected unitarity. We also provide a clearer understanding of predictions related to flux and cross-sections, taking into consideration any contamination from new physics affecting hadronic measurements. We focus on the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment to show that certain neutrino experiments have sensitivity to this issue. We discovered that certain constraints can limit deviation from expected neutrino behavior to below $10^{-3}$, exceeding current limits on a similar problem related to other subatomic particles. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Additionally, we predict that SHOWS will exhibit unique photoemission spectra and hinge state contributions to the specific heat and orbital susceptibility. This research provides a foundation for the theoretical investigation of other topological states powered by nonlinear operators and sets the stage for the development of showpiece 3D solid-state devices that harness the unique properties of showable states. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. All implementations utilize the free open-source platform FreeFEM3D. The algorithm addresses the issue of recovering data on an inaccessible boundary by formulating a quasi-reversibility problem. This approach leverages the boundary control problem formulation first introduced by Colton and Klein-Gordon equations. The method's success is evaluated through the relative error of the recovered data compared to the actual values, both in smooth and noisy cases. The project also compares different hybrid formulation advantages and disadvantages in terms of computational time and memory consumption. The research also explores the impact of mesh density on the algorithm's performance. The recovered data is analyzed in both magnitude and phase error aspects. The project's findings demonstrate the method's capability to effectively recover missing boundary data under various conditions. The algorithm's ability to handle two- and three-dimensional cases, with noisy input data, proves its robustness. The comparison of different hybrid formulation computational aspects provides valuable insights for future algorithm development. The impact of mesh density on the algorithm's performance validates the approach's flexibility. The analysis of the recovered data's magnitude and phase error under various conditions proves the method's reliability. The project's success in recovering missing boundary data based on incomplete boundary data and the comparison of different hybrid formulations provide a solid foundation for its application to related problems. This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with highest weight modules for integrable representations of the superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, a simple affine Lie superalgebra. We establish the underlying generators of this algebra in detail. Additionally, we obtain the explicit forms of the twisted multiplication and translation operators, as well as the quasi-particle structures of weighted highest weight modules for $osp(1|2n)$. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Furthermore, to facilitate widespread adoption, we made the code and data datasets available for public access. Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations. Furthermore, we explore and evaluate various theoretical frameworks that attempt to explain grid cells' underlying mechanisms and suggest avenues for future investigation. Ultimately, our review highlights the intricate and far-reaching implications of grid cells in the context of spatial navigation and suggests that a multidisciplinary approach is necessary to fully comprehend this intricate neural phenomenon. This review is accompanied by a set of experiments that use a spatial resolution task to evaluate the performance of models of grid cells and temporo-hippocampal place cells, revealing both the significance of accurate grid cell modeling and the potential for grid cells to underlie the index cells within the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As the field of neural navigation continues to evolve, further refinement of grid cell models will be crucial, driving greater understanding of the intricate mechanisms that govern spatial navigation within this renowned neural system. As a result of these improvements, we anticipate significant advancements in the ability of artificial neural networks to navigate complex environments, a key aspect that has been highlighted by the recent breakthroughs achieved by deep reinforcement learning systems. Ultimately, the capacity of an artificial neural network to navigate a diverse array of environments will continue to serve as a critical benchmark for evaluating its ability to learn the internal representations that underlie an animal's cognitive map. As such, we believe that studying grid cells, together with other index cells within the parahippocampal-hippocampal region, offers a rich opportunity for researchers at the intersection of neuroscience and artificial neural networks to collaborate and contribute to a deeper understanding of the intricate mechanisms that govern this renowned neural system. As such, we anticipate that the ongoing refinement of grid cell models will continue to drive innovative breakthroughs in artificial neural networks, directing researchers toward critical questions at the intersection of these two fields. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly specific dynamo processes. Consequently, we suggest that the presence of magnetic cycles in slow rotating solar-type stars should be assessed using global views of magnetic maps, rather than relying on traditional definitions based on the polarity configuration at a single point. This approach may provide further insights into the dynamo processes operating in these stars.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Notably, we find that for both unitary and non-unitary dynamics, the lowest-order terms of the distinguishability time can be understood in relation to the system's asymmetry or entanglement with its environment, respectively. Our findings provide valuable insights into the dynamics of qubit states and their separation from unitary and non-unitary evolutions. Furthermore, this work paves the way for exploring other open system dynamics in this context. By discussing several qubit states, we illustrate the significance of our results and offer potential directions for further research. The generalization of our findings to higher-dimensional systems is also considered. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Human-generated illustrations highlighting the device geometry and measurement setup are also provided, serving as a visual alternative to complex theoretical descriptions of dielectric functions. By combining theoretical modeling and experimental investigation, we assess the terahertz loss mechanisms in resonators, attributing them to carrier concentration in the silicon substrate, partially filled silicon etch, and aluminum loss. We demonstrate the utility of near-field terahertz investigation in identifying loss channels in quantum devices, setting the stage for utilizing this approach to regularly monitor and assess the integrity of quantum devices. This approach could become particularly useful within device development cycles, offering a more effective alternative to carrying out comprehensive theoretical analyses of complex device geometries. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. Alongside ongoing missions, we anticipate renewed interest in the planet following the successful entry into orbit of the Russian mission NVeza-Dzvyezdnaya Nauka, and the expected launch of the NASA VERITAS and UVGIS missions in 2028, which will offer fresh insights into the atmosphere's structure, composition, and surface interaction processes. Ultimately, a comprehensive understanding of these interactions is essential to predicting the planet's further evolution and addressing fundamental questions about Venus's development. The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior. Specifically, this method utilizes cell and tissue region features extracted from histology images to create HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue graphs. An associated neural network is designed to classify such graph representations, referred to as HACT-Net. As part of this work, a comprehensive dataset called the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset is created and employed to evaluate the efficacy of this method against pathologist assessments and current approaches. Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of this method over alternative techniques and even expert pathologist assessments in breast tumor subtyping tasks. In addition, comprehensive experiments are conducted to examine the impact of different components of the proposed method, including cell representation, tissue segmentation, region features, graph structure, and node ordering on its performance. Furthermore, this work introduces a unique approach to computing node orders for graph neural networks on histology cell graphs. An open-source implementation of this method is also made available as part of the Cytel Toolkit for Analyzing Histology Images. As a result, this method is an innovative solution for high-level tumor subtyping and can serve as a foundation for other applications involving multi-scale graph analysis in histology. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. Notably, this effectiveness of the Bayesian approach is evident even when the data are temporary and only reflect local behaviors of the process. As a result, the nonparametric Bayesian approach proves to be a powerful and versatile tool in analyzing the Hawkes process, facilitating the joint exploration of time-series data components and the underlying connectivity graph that drives the processes. We have implemented our methods in R through the package RTimeZyme, which is available for public use and can be utilized in conjunction with the RTimeZyme R package. The package RTimeZyme offers the nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process, including the granger connectivity graph, and provides additional functionality for generating artificial data, visualizing results, and employing various methods for survival analysis. The package RTimeZyme is accessible on CRAN. The RTimeZyme R package can be found at the following website: https://bbrazell.github.io/RTimeZyme/ The RTimeZyme R package is also available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/bbrazell/RTimeZyme The RTimeZyme R package has been used in the publication with arXiv ID: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17385, which is referenced in the package RTimeZyme. The RTimeZyme R package contains several important features, including the estimation of nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, the construction of Granger connectivity graphs, artificial data generation, visualization tools, and Bayesian estimation of the adjacency matrix. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. This modified algorithm has been made accessible through a publicly available code to facilitate further research in the field.
