Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations. The CS-CADA's code and data will be made available on https://github.com/zwang84/Cs-cada for further research community utilization. The proposed CS-CADA also surpasses the existing state-of-the-art methods in cross-anatomy domain adaptation by a notable margin according to comprehensive experimental results. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. Additionally, its unique properties make it susceptible to various applications, such as the enhancement of electromagnetic wave polarization and the possible creation of high-energy harmonic pulses. Furthermore, this component can also modulate the laser pulse duration, as indicated by our simulations, which show its potential as a pulse compressor. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Moreover, we explore the relationship between these structures and the original approach outlined by Godbillon. Along the way, we introduce the Godbillon-Villard class, a renowned example discussed in the field. Our study ultimately concludes with a discussion of the role that combinatorial differentiable manifolds may play in the context of the conjecture posed by Gelfand and MacPherson. This conjecture, which aims to circumvent the reliance on smooth structures in the calculation of Pontrjagin classes, appears to be compatible with the method proposed by Gelfand and MacPherson for combinatorial differentiable manifolds. This compatibility suggests that such structures might serve as a viable framework for calculating Pontrjagin classes under a particular assumption, only to discover that this assumption is already inherent in the premise itself. As a result, we propose rephrasing the conjecture for a more broadened context, which includes not only Pontrjagin classes but also other differential forms and a more extensive class of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. This revised version of the conjecture would then hold without any additional hypotheses. We also demonstrate that certain well-known examples, such as the Morsmith maps and the monodromy maps associated with singularity theories, are instances of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. This connection enables us to derive topological invariants for these maps. Furthermore, we establish that the Godbillon-Villard class is a closed form that can be carried over to the combinatorial differentiable manifold structure of a manifold, despite being originally defined through the differential structure of the manifold. This finding leads to a new interpretation of the Godbillon-Villard conjecture. We then prove that our proposed strategy for calculating Pontrjagin classes succeeds in a specific class of volumes over high-dimensional complex spaces, such as projective spaces. We hope that our study will provide a useful foundation for a more extensive investigation into Gelfand-MacPherson Conjecture.

SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. With MuLE, we estimate that the number of required image sensors could be reduced by a factor of ~30 in such missions. A prototype MuLE with a SiCAD2 sensor was constructed and is currently being tested on board the BaNaMa-S satellite, which was launched in December 2022. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Compared to traditional active learning methods, our selective labeling approach reduces labeling expenses by 90%. Our code and data are openly available for use at https://github.com/google-research-data/Selective-Labeling. Our technique has the added benefit of minimizing changes needed to existing active learning frameworks. This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under optimal, twice-switched control, the outcome is equivalent to that achieved through continuous control in both scenarios. Additionally, we highlight the significance of our findings by placing them within the broader context of swimmer dynamics. Finally, we suggest promising areas for exploration in future research.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Moreover, we find that dialogue behavior and sentiment can be predicted using a simple classification technique on the revised data set, thereby validating its utility for these tasks. Additionally, our results surpass previous best scores on sentiment prediction and joint behavior/sentiment prediction, as reported on the EMO20Q website. In addition to evaluating our method on the full data set, we also achieve comparable or better scores when employing various evaluation methods on several randomly selected subsets of the data set. Ultimately, our method has the added benefit of facilitating the understanding of label nuances by comparing the classification results with the classification outcomes obtained using the original data alone. We have made our code and data available at https://github.com/hahnfrg/emo20q-bert-annotation. Still, our approach's core contribution lies in showcasing that pre-trained language models can be utilized as reliable means of evaluating and revising intricate annotated data sets containing complex semantic labels. As such, we believe our method to be a significant step towards developing a more collective annotation process that incorporates these powerful models. Kopczyński (ICALP 2006) hypothesized that prefix-independence in half-positional winning conditions leads to closed unions. To disprove this hypothesis, we define a new set of bi-positional winning conditions known as 'energy conditions,' specifically tailored for totally ordered groups. Furthermore, we present an instance of two conditions within this new set whose union is not positionally significant. Building upon this finding, we theorize that any condition with this independence property shares similarities with energy conditions, especially those defined on totally ordered groups over cyclical sequences. Lastly, we formulate a stronger hypothesis that any condition with this independence property must resemble energy conditions across all structures, not just cyclical sequences. To support this stronger hypothesis, we offer an example of a game where a condition is positionally significant over all sequences, yet its union with energy-like conditions is not positionally significant. This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. Our evaluation will involve two different mesh configurations, with a focus on reducing the solid component to examine the RBM's performance. To further assess the methods, we'll consider a monolithic FSI approach on the same test case, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, with a focus on a Reynolds number of 100. To this end, we'll discuss the challenges associated with implementing these methods and present a comparative analysis of our results in terms of spatial and temporal convergence, as well as computational costs for both approaches. Additionally, we'll conduct a sensitivity analysis to examine the impact of different mesh sizes on our results. To facilitate easy replication of our findings, all necessary code and data will be made freely available as part of this project. Consequently, our open-access platform aims to provide a comprehensive starting point for researchers interested in the integration of RBM with FSI methods. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants. Additionally, our method identified the perpetrator with a macro F1 score of 0.4958 in subtask B, ranking 24th among 88 competitors. The underlying code for our analysis has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/aliyasghouy/UM-IU-LING for SemEval-2019-OffensEval.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This finding allows the design of sub-10 nm gaps with excellent electron confinement for optimizing spin-orbit coupling and spontaneous emission in metallic cavities. Furthermore, we show that a thorough understanding of electron spillover and nonlocal effects is crucial for developing reliable metal nanogaps utilizing electron spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation. Ultimately, our research provides valuable guidelines for the design of metal nanogaps with precise electron confinement and controlled interaction with light at a deep-solid-state interface.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Additionally, the evolution of the Calculus of Constructions is outlined in conjunction with key developments in dependently typed programming and the underlying computer science related to these advancements. This survey's comprehensive historical and technical overview is beneficial to programmers, advanced computer science students, and researchers in the field. The authors provide relevant background information and the current state of dependently typed programming and the Calculus of Constructions for those seeking more in-depth information. This survey is presented in a clear, accessible manner, making it an ideal introduction to the subject matter for programmers, advanced computer science students, and researchers in the field. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. Furthermore, the study highlights the complex YSR state splitting as a sensitive indicator of the local magnetic dimer's character. Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at an optical distance of around 5 from the cloud's boundary, allowing for more efficient use of computational resources and potential improvements to reconstruction algorithms. To test this new approach, we developed a simulated experiment using the SNB code, a comprehensive model of three-dimensional cloud dynamics. The results of this experiment highlighted the importance of accounting for the core extinction scale and suggested that more targeted reconstruction methods could enhance the accuracy of cloud tomography. Nonetheless, addressing the fundamental limitations of this approach, such as the scattering problem, will be essential for advancing cloud tomography. To this end, we propose a strategy for prioritizing the development of novel three-dimensional radiative transfer codes that can handle complex cloud cores, as well as improve the representation of particle size and optical thickness within these cores. Ultimately, this work aims to lay the groundwork for a new paradigm in cloud tomography, one that acknowledges the core extinction scale and fuels the development of more effective codes capable of handling complex cloud morphology. The path forward for these codes will depend on simulations that account for the effects of particle asymmetry and multiplicity, as well as further research into the core's scattering properties, particularly for larger particles. Despite the complexity of this problem, we believe that the core extinction scale represents a critical opportunity for advancing both cloud tomography and three-dimensional radiative transfer codes, enabling a new generation of accurate cloud assessments that can match the complexity of real cloud morphology. The future of these codes will depend on a deeper understanding of how to utilize computational resources to streamline solvers for complex cloud cores, as well as a more effective use of high-performance computing to tackle the challenges posed by cloud tomography. We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear variation. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target before the lower frequency component, whereas the reverse occurs in positive frequency variations. As a result, a more densely packed plasma is needed for transmission with negative frequency variations, as opposed to unchirped or positively chirped pulses. However, negative frequency variations allow for increased transmission at higher densities (six times the critical density), producing a highly stable and persistent electrostatic field behind the target and significant ion acceleration in opposite directions due to the electron void. Additionally, our experiment features an auxiliary thin layer with low density, situated behind the main target layer. Ions from the auxiliary layer can be efficiently accelerated into a mono-energetic beam by the electrostatic field generated in the main target under interaction with a negatively frequency-modulated, highly intense laser pulse, achieving protons with maximum energies of around 100 MeV when subjected to specific optimal conditions involving a 10-fs, intensively Gaussian pulse with 8.5 times ten to the power of twenty watts per square centimeter peak intensity. Our experimental findings demonstrate the potential of frequency-modulated laser pulses for multifaceted ion beam generation in experiments related to heavy ion research.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. This system provides scientists with a chance to study how young planets evolve and interact with their surroundings through gravitational processes. Ultimately, TOI-712's planetary system may offer insights into the development of giant planets and the longevity of small planets in low-mass star systems. By conducting radial velocity and spectroscopic analyses, the team learned that the system contains a substantial amount of material being ejected from the planet-sstar interaction, amounting to $0.45\pm0.26$ Earth masses, and is directed towards the planet with the longest orbital period. This finding suggests that the system contains a significant amount of angular momentum, which can shed light on the planets' formation history. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Additionally, our study reveals that nitrogen defects are more stable in both substitutional and interstitial forms, and that the formation energy of interstitial N is lower than that of carbon by approximately 0.05eV.  Conversely, the formation energy of substitutional carbon is lower than that of nitrogen by approximately 0.1eV.  We attribute these differences to the larger size of carbon atoms which makes substitutional carbon more difficult to incorporate into the TiO2 lattice.  Finally, we calculate the diffusion energies of these defects, and find that both carbon and nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess high diffusion energies, while defects positioned substitutionally possess lower diffusion energies, consistent with their lower formation energies.  These outcomes could serve as a basis for further investigation and modeling of carbon and nitrogen defects in TiO2.

I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Additionally, this research introduces the concept of distal groups, defined as those with no polynomial diameter generating sets and shows that such groups have multiple intersecting, non-conjugate subgroups. It also demonstrates that distal groups are extensive and include many well-known groups, such as the BAUMSLY-SHALEV group and the symmetric group S_n in its natural representation, among others. Furthermore, this research shows that the scale of a group's abelian section can serve as a bound for its diameter, and it is hypothesized that this relationship could be nearly linear. To support this hypothesis, several additional lower diameter bounds are established for specific groups, such as the diagonal subgroup of the BAUMSLY-SHALEV group and the solvable permutation group designed by Guralnik. These results raise intriguing questions about the complex interplay between a group's geometric structure and its conjugacy class pattern. Moreover, this research offers several open problems and conjectures on this topic, particularly regarding the relationship between a group's diameter and its conjugacy class size and structure. These questions have significant implications for our understanding of finite groups in relation to polynomial expansion and its connections to Lie groups, and they are certain to stimulate further in-depth research in this field.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. To enhance the system's reliability, a static error correction technique is also proposed and verified through experiments. This temperature sensor module demonstrates superior performance compared to leading CMOS temperature sensors, showcasing its immense potential for adaptive voltage and frequency scaling systems. Moreover, this research proposes the sensor module as a versatile temperature-to-digitally-analogue converter, capable of generating two distinct analogue outputs with proportional frequencies for frequency-modulated analogue-to-digitally-analogue converters. The design's versatility, coupled with its outstanding performance, makes it an ideal solution for a wide range of complex thermal monitoring systems. In our research, we'll detail the design and development of Pied Piper, introducing a novel query-language that incorporates lyrics and music-related operators to facilitate precise audio content retrieval. We'll also present results from two separate usability assessments, showcasing how our innovative approach outperforms traditional search engines in accordance with user preferences. Furthermore, we highlight Pied Piper's comprehensive music database and discuss potential future developments, including the integration of additional music content and personalized music recommendations. This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375], the study establishes connections between key concepts within the field. Notably, a significant correlation between gerbes over stacks has been established in [arXiv:1907.00375], the development of the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids equipped with a connection has been introduced in [arXiv:2012.08447], the relationship between connections on principal bundles over Deligne Mumford stacks has been examined through the Atiyah sequence in [arXiv:2012.08442], and topological groupoid extensions were defined along with their correspondence to gerbes over topological stacks in [arXiv:2103.04560]. The research also sees the investigation of bundle gerbes over Lie groupoids equipped with a left action, the construction of twisted bundle gerbes, and the study of twisted bundle gerbes over Deligne-Mumford stacks. Additionally, a framework for introducing bundle gerbes over stacky groupoids has been established and applied to a theoretical framework for quantum field theories on suitable singular spacetimes. The framework includes the definition of twisted bundle gerbes and their correspondence to twisted gerbes over stacks in [arXiv:2103.04560]. The research is further illustrated through the computation of a twisted Chern-Connes-Kasparian character for twisted bundle gerbes over Deligne-Mumford stacks. The associated paper on the twisted CCK characer for gerbes over stacks has been submitted to [arXiv:2206.04096]. The study also sees the introduction of a twisted crossed product of gerbes over Deligne-Mumford stacks and the investigation of a quantum field theory based on a super-symmetric Yang-Mills Chern-Simons theory in [arXiv:2206.04097]. The related research on super-symmetric Yang-Mills Chern-Simons theory has been presented at the conference [arXiv:2206.04098]. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  In addition, we observe a substantial increase in the mass of cores within the Dragon cloud compared to typical infrared dark clouds, such as the G25.11-0.89 IRDC.  We also discover a prominent core mass function slope of 2.0 within the Dragon cloud, which can be explained by the presence of massive protostellar cores.  Finally, we find evidence suggesting that the core mass function may be influenced by the availability of massive parent molecular clouds, as illustrated by a core mass function correlation between the Dragon cloud and a comparison set of infrared dark clouds.  This cloud-proper volume effect could have a significant impact on the interpretation of core mass functions in regional and global spectra.  Therefore, it is crucial to consider the environmental factors of massive star-forming regions when analyzing the core mass function and the resulting star formation, as these regions may be influenced by selective core destruction based on mass.  This destruction would result in an artificially increased core mass function slope and a apparent mass accumulation in protostellar cores, as seen in the Dragon cloud.  Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for a comprehensive investigation of the core mass function in a regional and global context, including an examination of the core-sphere relation and the influence of core destruction on star-forming regions.  This study paves the way for a deeper understanding of the complex interplay among core mass function, star formation, and the massive parent molecular clouds, as well as the core-sphere relation, by exploring the core mass function within the Dragon cloud and comparing it with a set of infrared dark clouds, and also investigating the selective core destruction in the Dragon cloud, the largest infrared dark cloud known so far, based on a statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores.

The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators. These results can be viewed as duals of correspondence theory conducted on the operator version of finite forest models. The study also explores quasivarieties within the context of Godel modal logic with operators. The results are represented through algebraic and relational semantics for first-order Godel modal logic with the Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse style technique, leading to a proof of a Godel modal logic counterpart to the result of Buedenbender. The research also examines the expressiveness of language involving the loveliness property, known as prelinearity, and discovers instances where it is sufficient for other loveliness properties to hold. Secondly, the study proves that the class of finite Godel algebras is a variety using a method different from that of Galton. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Moreover, we find that using contextual information yields higher accuracy rates across almost all feature engineering methods tested. Ultimately, our research provides insights into the classification of LiDAR data and suggests avenues for further exploration. The associated code has been made publicly available for the benefit of the LiDAR classification community. This study evaluates multiple classification approaches for LiDAR data, incorporating multiple machine learning algorithms and context-based techniques. Our analysis reveals that using neighboring point information and feature engineering boosts accuracy and encourages further research in this area. To support the LiDAR classification community, the associated code has been made publicly available.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. Additionally, this paper explores novel operator constructions, utilizing a fractional differential operator, and proves the existence of a related system of orthogonal polynomials. Consequently, this discovery enables the characterization of the (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions on the sphere, allowing for a dimension increase of one. This breakthrough, rooted in the fundamental theory of special functions, can be applied to develop innovative algorithms for the construction of strictly positive definite functions. As a result, this will have a significant impact on various numerical techniques, such as the discretization of boundary value problems and the construction of sampling operators in the context of boundary integral equations. As a by-product, this paper also reveals the uniqueness of the obtained system of orthogonal polynomials and explores its connections to the classical Jacobi and Laguerre polynomials. The associated operator constructions, linked to the derivative and integral of the Gegenbauer polynomials, are critical to the proposed methodology. As the underlying space dimension increases by one, the obtained system of orthogonal polynomials exhibits a unique rotation invariance, linked to the classical system of the confluent hypergeometric polynomials, namely the Jacobi, Laguerre, and Hermite polynomials. Consequently, this rotation invariance is shown to result in the introduction of a new system of orthogonal polynomials, closely related to the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness for a dimension increase of one. As the underlying space dimension increases by two, the characteristics of this system of orthogonal polynomials will be addressed in the companion paper. The concepts developed in this paper have far-reaching implications for various applications, such as the construction of positive definite functions employed in the discretization of boundary value problems and the construction of sampling operators in boundary integral equations. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications. We've also derived an expression for average dissipated energy in terms of an equilibrium correlation energy, revealing that it serves as a fundamental thermodynamic properties descriptor. Furthermore, we show that this expression holds true for harmonic oscillators with multiple degrees of freedom, both numerically and analytically. Our study highlights the importance of defining microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics in relation to each other by using reversible processes in phase space, and demonstrates that average dissipated energy represents a fundamental thermodynamic properties marker that requires further exploration in different systems. We believe that extending these concepts to open systems will provide valuable insights into understanding nonequilibrium thermodynamic processes. We also find that the proposed method can be applied to monitor energy dissipation dynamics in simulations of systems undergoing contraction or expansion, facilitating the development of new thermodynamic algorithms that minimize residual energy, particularly for Monte Carlo simulations. We illustrate the benefits of our approach by enhancing the performance of two Monte Carlo simulations, one for binary mixtures and the other for harmonic oscillators with multiple degrees of freedom, by utilizing the proposed definition of microstate work. We anticipate that this work will contribute to advancing the development of nonequilibrium thermodynamic algorithms that prioritize energy minimization. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. The proposed models also achieve superior performance without increasing computational complexity. We also analyze our results by examining the distribution of look-ahead attention weights and the performance with training data restrictions. The success of our proposals indicates that the translation process can be viewed as a process of interacting between target words, and further motivates closer examination of the temporal relationships between target words in machine translation. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Finally, we outline promising areas for further research and development in this space. Among them are methods for assessing the quality of grid applications, techniques for cooperative problem-solving, and tools for creating virtual organizations. With more groups joining the grid computing research community due in part to the introduction of grid schools, we believe it is time to take a step back and evaluate the state of the field. In doing so, we hope to motivate others to join the effort and explore the many opportunities available in this area. Therefore, it may also be a suitable introduction to the subject for newcomers to the field. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures. This research is further underscored by an open-source implementation that is freely accessible and configurable across various undirected graphs, including those based on real-world data. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside a reliability boost of at least 31.1% compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, this approach reduces the coverage gap between theoretical maximum coverage and practical coverage by at least 13.9%. Our optimized routing approach achieves a coverage optimization ratio of up to 126.1% better than routing methods alone. The sensitivity analysis reveals that the sensitivity of this approach is 97.2% reliable when the sensitivity of individual vehicles is 90%, indicating robust performance in face of declining sensor accuracy. A notable outcome of this research is the obtained dataset, a uniquely structured rural and urban road network dataset, based on real-world data from New York City, available for public use and potential application in the field of mobile sensing and data analysis. This research paves the way for a revolutionary concept of "roads as a service" where city roads can be monitored, managed, and maintained through a mobile sensing approach by rideharing vehicle fleets acting as co-operators. This study provides a theoretical foundation and practical implementation, making it accessible for other cities to adapt and utilize this innovative mobile sensing approach. The developed framework, routing optimization algorithm, and derived insights are all compatible with general road network topology, allowing other cities to employ this approach by substituting the New York City data with their own respective data. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis. Additionally, we show that our new methods have similar order conditions to existing first derivative general linear methods when using uniform grids. This research further enlarges the family of SGLMs and makes them more versatile.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, scores are often dictated by these phrases alone, rendering the model over-stable and ineffective. Interestingly, our study discovered a stark contrast between this outcome and that of other probing studies examining how well these types of pre-trained models grasp more subtle linguistic aspects such as syntax, morphology, and parts-of-speech. Additionally, we identified a further issue: the autoscoring models developed biases towards the data used during training, resulting in over-sensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose the use of detection-based protection models that are highly accurate at detecting samples with anomalous attribution patterns or characteristics of manipulable data, thus enabling the identification of suspicious scores with higher effectiveness. Our findings are relevant not only to the specific autoscoring models investigated but also to any other scoring systems developed using similar deep learning technologies. As such, they are likely to be informative for any related research probing the workings of complex deep learning models. This research is further enriched by the inclusion of additional analysis and investigative pathways that are recommended for further exploration in future studies. The data, models, and tools used in this study are available for replication purposes. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To achieve this, the authors split a typical U-Net architecture into two components: a first component that extracts dense features, capable of delivering density masks, and a second component that extracts boundary features, used to obtain binary masks from the density masks. To further enhance model performance, the authors employed a strategy in which two identical models with the same architecture were trained on alternate image patches to detect nuclei in different directions. As a result, this approach achieved outstanding performance on the public NSCLC-pathological dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin, and resulting in a model capable of accurate cell detection. A thorough analysis of model performance was conducted through experiments on the public NSCLC-pathological dataset, with the evaluation of different model architectures, performance on fused cell annotation, and model robustness tested in real-world cancer diagnosis scenarios. In conclusion, this study introduces a groundbreaking W-shaped network, which has demonstrated exceptional performance on the public NSCLC-pathological dataset, has outstanding cell detection capabilities, and has achieved state-of-the-art results in various benchmark datasets. The source code for this study has been made available on GitHub. In addition to this approach, the authors have released a public dataset containing fused cell annotations, which will serve as a reference point for the detection of complex cells

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. Furthermore, refined protocols for bulletproofs and a quantum-resistant key exchange scheme have been successfully implemented using HELMHOLTZ. The innovative approach of this project also enables the detection of Michelson programs behaving maliciously, a key feature that sets it apart from other static verification tools. The development of refined protocols and the detection of malicious programs are made possible by a novel use of refinement types that extends beyond protocol validation alone. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Our research offers a comprehensive, unified explanation of GCNNs within the context of irregular data patterns and provides a graphical representation of learning within such networks. A corresponding Python code is also available for experimenting with GCNNs through the Matplotlib library. As the underlying logic of GCNNs is now more thoroughly understood, future improvements could potentially focus on developing new convolutional elements tailored to specific recognition tasks. The underlying principles of GCNNs also provide a versatile framework for teaching intermediate-level Deep Learning concepts. The overall goal of this work is to promote further exploration into the fundamental aspects of GCNNs, making it suitable for publication in the 2021 IEEE Circuits and Systems Magazine. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Additionally, VSSA beamforming, combined with OVERWIND, demonstrates notable improvements in the estimation of mechanical properties, namely elasticity and anisotropy. Notably, VSSA beamforming produces comparable results to the established SA technique using focused transmitted data, while VSSA's increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies enable accurate elastography in low signal-to-noise ratio scenarios. Experimental outcomes validate the study's simulation-based findings, revealing notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement and mechanical properties. The VSSA beamforming technique presents a viable elastography imaging modality. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This, in turn, enables the generation of executable code across a given set of initial inputs and logically derived outputs. Our approach is then applied to a game design, a linguistic framework known as Game Logical Programming, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our method by solving a complex problem involving the creation of interactive drama. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm's coreset size estimate is accurate to within a factor of $\Delta$, which represents the maximum distance between any two points in the dataset. Building upon this finding, we derive an algorithm that provides a precise size estimate for the coreset, utilizing approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$ storage, and offers a factor of $\Delta$ accuracy. By incorporating this algorithm into our framework, we can obtain the coreset directly without needing to know the value of $\Delta$. The resulting algorithm utilizes approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $k$ storage, providing a precise size estimate for the coreset. Finally, we demonstrate that our algorithms for the $k$-means clustering problem can be applied to settings where data points are defined as elements of a metric space, without requiring significant increases in storage complexity. The latter observation complements our experimentally-derived findings, which demonstrated that the storage requirements of previous algorithms scale quadratically with the dimensionality of the space in practice, highlighting the importance of our theoretical contribution in this context. The proposed algorithms are supported by experimental evaluations, conducted using both synthetic data and real-world datasets, to further illustrate their effectiveness. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Additionally, we observe that our method's best performances are matched by flat policies in certain cases, but overall, it offers a versatile solution for large-scale discrete stochastic PEGs. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. 

Additionally, our work involves an examination of 'nontransitive' triples within specified constraints, and provides computational tools to facilitate the evaluation of special cases. Our findings demonstrate a tendency for the middle element to approach 0.5 as the number of elements increases without bound. 

Our research offers a counterintuitive insight, revealing instances where the largest element is almost certain to surpass the smallest one, yet the likelihood of the middle element being greater than both is essentially negligible, especially as the number of elements increases without bound. 

Our work is further distinguished by our introduction of order-crossing probabilities, and the novel expressions we derive to explain various symmetric properties. 

Finally, our investigation includes an examination of the relationship between the special case of random triples and an associated game, and provides an analysis of the strategy that ensures the maximum likelihood of winning this game. 

Our research is an expansion of the 2003 paper by Klaus Ambrosch and Bernd Pahnke, and offers an updated perspective on this topic as well as an exploration of newly identified parameters.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Moreover, the proposed architecture achieves greater flexibility, enabling the enhancement of various CT images with different dose levels, and can also be applied to super-resolution CT image enhancement. With enhanced stability and better generalization, our method requires only a single training process without needing to re-optimize parameters for different training datasets. Consequently, the proposed switchable cycleGAN algorithm delivers outstanding performance when evaluated using public datasets, and is therefore highly suitable for enhancing a broad range of CT images, particularly those in the abdomen. Additionally, the easy conversion feature makes it an incredibly useful technique for various clinical applications. The code for the proposed method has been made available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/zwang84/SSG-ZESIC. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes.

This research aims to examine the geometric makeup of an ideal fluid's spacetime 
when coupled with a torsion-forming vector field and the relationship between the 
conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric and the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe metric. We first 
derive conditions for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton to be in a state of 
expansion, stability, or contraction. Subsequently, we establish a Laplace 
equation using the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe soliton when the soliton's potential 
vector field is a gradient type. Additionally, this research relates an ideal 
fluid's spacetime to a Robertson-Walker spacetime and discusses various physics 
and gravitational implications. We then discuss future research prospects. 

Keywords: Ideal fluid spacetime, conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton, eta-Ricci-Yamabe 
soliton, Laplace equation, Robertson-Walker spacetime. 

Abstract: This study involves an ideal fluid spacetime coupled with a torsion-forming 
vector field and examines the geometric structure of an ideal fluid's spacetime 
when its potential vector field is a conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton. We establish 
a relationship between the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton and the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe 
soliton. We derive conditions for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton to be in a 
state of expansion, stability, or contraction. We then discuss future research 
prospects on this topic. 

When the soliton's potential vector field is a gradient type, we derive a Laplace

case of the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton. Therefore, all the conditions for the 
conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe soliton to be in a state of expansion, stability, or 
contraction are also applicable to the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton.
