Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. The available code and studies will allow for the generation of more accurate collective effects of weak bosons, encompassing both forward radiation and weak boson fusion/scattering, facilitating a deeper comprehension of the fundamental characteristics of colliders operating at energies beyond a few TeV. The effective incorporation of W/Z PDFs is expected to significantly contribute to the advancement of theoretical description of these colliders when considering 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Our study's outcomes provided camera system designers with with valuable insights into AI-based calibration methods and their limitations, potentially leading to their deployment in real-world robotic vision applications. Additionally, we made the code and data associated with the study openly available for further development.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Our approach demonstrates the capability to create realistic samples in real-time, given the versatility of GANs, and provides a reliable solution for solving complex inverse problems involving incomplete or noisy data. A comprehensive analysis, including a study on the effect of measurement noise and a comparison to a state-of-the-art method, is also included in the report. A publicly accessible implementation of the proposed method is also available online.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. We conclude by discussing the crucial role that invariant manifolds play in the analysis of the long-term behavior of dynamical systems. We also provide examples illustrating stability, coexistence, and switching dynamics in fractional-order systems with linear subspaces as invariant manifolds. We hope that this survey will provide a useful resource for researchers looking to explore the fundamental role of stability in the context of invariant sets. Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. To tackle this optimization problem in the presence of channel state uncertainty and noise, a reinforcement learning solution inspired by the multi-armed bandit problem is proposed. Simulations show the new technique converges quickly in dynamic channel conditions and offers up to 75% better performance than conventional methods in terms of spectral efficiency. The technique is also tested under non-linear power amplification scenarios and shown to maintain its optimal performance. The proof of convergence for the reinforcement learning solution is verified through numerical examples, and the technique is validated through simulations under time-varying channels. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. The screen at about 12.58 parsecs distance appears to be linked to the G179.0+7.3 supern remnant, and may comprise a potential remnant shell. The third screen, located at around 2.56 parsecs, is more complicated to interpret due to potential associations with the Taurus molecular cloud or the beta Pictoris molecular circle. The distinct nature of these screens, particularly the medium-sized one associated with the G179.0+7.3 remnant, makes them amenable to further study through variability observations and potential connections to other physical phenomena. Furthermore, Arecibo's replacement by the Extremely Large Telescope or the Square Kilometre Array will provide even more detailed data for in-depth analysis of these scattering screens and others like them. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a greater understanding of the interstellar medium and its interaction with the motion of stars and other celestial objects across the galaxy. By examining screens at various distances, it is possible to construct a three-dimensional view of the interstellar medium and its structure. In return, screens can also be affected by the emission and absorption of light from nearby stars, making them effective tools for studying the physics of the surrounding environment. The ongoing and planned advancements in telescopic technology will provide a wealth of new information for in-depth analysis of these scattering screens, offering a chance to construct a three-dimensional view of the interstellar medium and its components. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, a subjective test confirms that QPNet can improve both naturalness and pitch accuracy compared to WN and a baseline method. The source codes for QPNet are available online at https://github.com/ghulghule/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Moreover, this relationship enables the derivation of shadows for bicategories obtained through Morita equivalence, essentially providing a way to compute the shadows of a bicategory without having to compute THH directly. Additionally, this framework is applied to demonstrate the functorial nature of THH in a more intuitive manner. Finally, with the concept of shadows, it is shown how THH can be applied to bicategories that are not abelian, such as the category of complexes of abelian groups. As a result, this approach offers a more general framework for understanding THH of bicategories and enables the computation of shadows for bicategories that are equivalent to others through Morita equivalence. As an example, this is demonstrated for the bicategories of finite dimensional Lie algebras and their representations. As another example, this is shown for the bicategories obtained from the category of super finite dimensional Lie algebras and their representations. As a further development, this framework is applied to derive shadows for the THH of abelian bicategories that are obtained through extension closed limits and functors, such as limits and pull-backs. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. The code and models are available for download at https://github.com/tongsongzheng/Sound-Source-Localization. The VGG-Sound Source dataset can be found at https://shanghaidata.org/vgg-sound-source.html.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Moreover, LGCN achieves a notable 5.45% improvement in accuracy on unsupervised graph clustering, and it effectively identifies the hierarchy of nodes by hyperbolic path tracing. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Additionally, this framework includes a control system where the source term represents a control input, and we can establish both uniqueness and controllability of the system. This result is attained through a combination of the stability estimate and a previous paper on the controllability of the same PDE model without the source term, as well as a recent paper on the controllability of a similar system with an additional advection term. Consequently, we can establish the stability of both the direct and inverse problems implemented with a finite difference discretization. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This choice of gauge can be viewed as a particular limit of the Einstein action, where the coefficient of the higher derivative term in the action is chosen such that the harmonic gauge is achieved in a massless regime. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. 

Furthermore, we found D-poor hydrogen isotopic signatures in the magnesium-rich core fragments of the Chelyabinsk meteorite, which can be interpreted as an indication of the formation of iron and magnesium cores before the delivery of volatile elements. This result supports previous research on the pre-accretionary hydrogen isotopic composition of Solar System materials, suggesting a D-poor hydrogen value of -433±107. 

In addition, we determined the D/H isotopic ratio in the Antarctic chondrites, which fell within the range of previous analyses, and found no significant differences in the water content and D/H isotope ratios in the pyroxene and plagioclase minerals from the same chondrite finds. This finding indicates that the variations in D/H isotope ratios in the chondrites are likely the result of the incorporation of hydrogen isotopes from different presolar grains rather than the redistribution of water within the chondrite particles during thermal metamorphism.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate increased efficacy in domains with limited data (<5000 sentences). Our findings facilitate further research into zero-shot speech-to-text and multi-task learning in speech and text. Our code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/Zero-Shot-Speech-to-Text. Our models are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/ghrua.

Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The framework we introduce also enables a more accurate determination of model parameters for systems exhibiting $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, such as niobium and palladium based materials. For instance, we demonstrate that in NbO$_2$, a model that incorporates $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing yields a higher effective spin-orbit coupling than the standard $t_{2g}$ only model, leading to a higher total magnetic moment and orbital occupation ratio, in line with experimental observations. The tools we develop to analyze $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixed-state magnetism can be adapted to other systems with analogous orbital crossings in transition metal compounds.
